"But the truth is," the gentleman continued, with a half smile towards the silent President of the bank, "there was nothing in this box that would have been of much use to any other parties than ourselves. If there had been a bond or so here, I doubt if we should have come off so fortunately, eh? The lock has evidently been wrenched open, and that is certainly a pretty sure sign that something is not right hereabouts."

"Something is decidedly wrong," came from Mr. Sylvester sternly; "but through whose fault we do not as yet know." And with a few words expressive of his relief at finding the other had sustained no material loss, he allowed the agent to depart.

===Chinese===
「不过实情是，」那位先生接着说，朝那位始终沉默的行长投以半带笑意的一瞥，「这匣子里原没有什么东西，于我们之外的旁人能派上多大用场。倘或这里头有一两张债券，我便怀疑我们能否这般幸运地了事了，嗯？锁眼一看便是被硬撬开的，这无疑是个相当可靠的征兆，说明左近必有蹊跷。」

「确有蹊跷。」西尔维斯特先生严厉地发话，「可究竟是谁的过错，我们尚且不知。」他说了几句，对这位先生未受实利上的损失表示宽慰，便让那位代办告辞了。

===Original===
He had no sooner left the room than Mr. Stuyvesant rose. "Are you going to question Hopgood now?" queried he, nervously pocketing his notebook.

"Yes sir, if you have no objections."

The director fidgeted with his chair and finally moved towards the door.

"I think you will get along better with him alone," said he. "He is a man who very easily gets embarrassed, and has a way of acting as if he were afraid of me. I will just step outside while you talk to him."

But Mr. Sylvester with a sudden dark flush on his brow, hastily stopped him. "I beg you will not," said he, with a quick realization of what Hopgood might be led to say in the forthcoming interview, if he were not restrained by the presence of the director. "Hopgood is not so afraid of you that he will not answer every question that is put to him with straightforward frankness." And he pushed up a chair, with a smile that Mr. Stuyvesant evidently found himself unable to resist. The screen trembled slightly, but none of them noticed it; Mr. Sylvester at once rang for Hopgood.

===Chinese===
他前脚刚离屋，斯泰弗森特先生便站起身来。「您现在就要盘问霍普古德了么？」他问道，紧张地把笔记本塞回口袋。

「是的，先生——您若不反对。」

那位董事在椅子上不安地挪动了一阵，终于朝门口移步。

「我想您独自一人同他谈会更顺手些。」他说，「他这人动辄便窘迫，那一副做派，倒像是很怕我似的。你们谈着，我便到外头去避一避。」

可西尔维斯特先生额上忽然浮起一片阴沉的红潮，急忙把他拦住。「我求您别走。」他说——猛然意识到，若无这位董事在场约束，霍普古德在那即将开始的问话里，可能被引着说出什么话来。「霍普古德并不至于怕您怕到那种地步，凡问他的话，他都会以直率的坦诚作答。」他把一张椅子往前推了推，脸上挂着笑意——斯泰弗森特先生显然觉得难以推却。屏风微微颤动了一下，但他们谁也不曾留意；西尔维斯特先生随即拉铃传霍普古德。

===Original===
He came in panting with his hurried descent from the fifth story, his face flushed and his eyes rolling, but without any of the secret perturbation Bertram had observed in them on a former occasion. "He cannot help us," was the thought that darkened the young man's brow as his eyes left the janitor, and faltering towards his uncle, fell upon the table before him.

Everything was reflected in the mirror.

"Well, Hopgood, I have a few questions to put to you this morning," said Mr. Sylvester in a restrained, but not unkindly tone.

The worthy man bowed, bestowed a salutatory roll of his eyes on Mr. Stuyvesant, and stood deferentially waiting.

"No, he cannot help us," was again Bertram's thought, and again his eyes faltered to his uncle's face, and again fell anxiously before him.

"It has not been my habit to trouble you with inquiries about your management of matters under your charge," continued Mr. Sylvester, stopping till the janitor's wandering eyes settled upon his own. "Your conduct has always been exemplary, and your attention to duty satisfactory; but I would like to ask you today if you have observed anything amiss with the vaults of late? anything wrong about the boxes kept there? anything in short, that excited your suspicion or caused you to ask yourself if everything was as it should be?"

===Chinese===
他从五楼一路赶下来，进门时还在喘气，脸涨得通红，眼珠不停地转——可那双眼里并不含伯特兰上回所察觉到的隐秘慌乱。「他帮不了我们。」这便是那年轻人眉头之所以阴沉起来的心事——他的目光从看门人身上移开，迟疑地朝叔父那边去，最后落到面前的桌上。

这一切都映在了镜子里。

「喂，霍普古德，今早我有几句话要问你。」西尔维斯特先生以一种有所收敛、却并不严苛的口吻说道。

这一位厚道人鞠了一躬，把那一双用以致意的眼珠朝斯泰弗森特先生转了转，便恭敬地站着等候。

「不，他帮不了我们。」伯特兰又起了这个念头，目光又迟疑地飘到叔父脸上，又焦灼地落到面前去。

「拿你职责之内的事来盘问、扰你不安，这从来不是我的习惯。」西尔维斯特先生接着说，他停了停，直到看门人那双游移的眼睛落到自己眼中。「你向来行事无可挑剔，奉职尽责，令我称意；可今日我倒想问你一句——近来你可曾察觉保险库有何异样？那里存放的匣子可有什么不对头之处？简而言之，可有什么引起了你的疑心，或令你自问一切是否果真如其所应是？」

===Original===
The janitor's ruddy face grew pale, and his eye fell with startled inquiry on Mr. Harrington's box that still occupied the centre of the table. "No, sir," he emphatically replied, "has anything—"

But Mr. Sylvester did not wait to be questioned. "You have attended to your duties as promptly and conscientiously as usual; you have allowed no one to go to the vaults day or night, who had no business there? You have not relaxed your accustomed vigilance, or left the bank alone at any time during the hours it is under your charge?"

"No sir, not for a minute, sir; that is—" He stopped and his eye wandered towards Mr. Stuyvesant. "Never for a minute, sir," he went on, "without I knew someone was in the bank, who was capable of looking after it."

===Chinese===
那看门人红润的脸变了白，目光吃了一惊、带着探询落到仍占据桌中央的哈灵顿先生的匣子上。「没有，先生。」他着力地答道，「可是出了什么——」

可西尔维斯特先生不等他反问。「你照旧勤勉尽责地料理着自己的差事；无论昼夜，你都不曾让任何与此无干之人走到保险库去，是么？你不曾松懈素来的警觉，也不曾在这银行归你看守的时辰里，把它独自撇下过？」

「没有，先生，一瞬也没有，先生；这就是说——」他打住了，眼珠朝斯泰弗森特先生那边溜了过去。「一瞬也没有，先生，」他接着说，「除非我晓得行里另有人，能照看它。」

===Original===
"The watchman has been at his post every night up to the usual hour?"

"Yes sir."

"There has been no carelessness in closing the vault doors after the departure of the clerks?"

"No sir."

"And no trouble," he continued, with a shade more of dignity, possibly because Hopgood's telltale face was beginning to show signs of anxious confusion, "and no trouble in opening them at the proper time each morning?"

"No sir."

"One question more—"

===Chinese===
「守夜人夜夜都守到惯常那个钟点才走？」

「是的，先生。」

「办事员散值之后，关保险库门未曾有过疏忽？」

「没有，先生。」

「也未曾有过——」他接着说，平添了几分威严——这或许是因为霍普古德那张藏不住事的脸，开始现出焦灼慌乱之色了——「也未曾有过什么麻烦，每天早上按时把它们打开？」

「没有，先生。」

「再问一句——」

===Original===
But here Bertram was called out, and in the momentary stir occasioned by his departure, Hopgood allowed himself to glance at the box before him more intently than he had hitherto presumed to do. He saw it was unlocked, and his hands began to tremble. Mr. Sylvester's voice recalled him to himself.

"You are a faithful man," said that gentleman, continuing his speech of a minute before, "and as such we are ready to acknowledge you; but the most conscientious amongst us are sometimes led into indiscretions. Now have you ever through carelessness or by means of any inadvertence, revealed to anyone in or out of the bank, the particular combination by which the lock of the vault-door is at present opened?"

"No sir, indeed no; I am much too anxious, and feel my own responsibility entirely too much, not to preserve so important a secret with the utmost care and jealousy."

===Chinese===
可就在这时，伯特兰被人叫了出去；趁他离场那一阵短暂的骚动，霍普古德大着胆子朝面前的匣子看了过去，比他此前所敢的还要专注。他看出那匣子没上锁，两只手便开始打颤。西尔维斯特先生的声音把他唤了回来。

「你是个忠心人。」那位先生接着一分钟前的话头说道，「正因如此，我们也愿意这样承认你；可我们之中最尽责的人，有时也免不了行出不慎之举。那么你可曾——无论出于疏忽、或出于某种不经意——向行内或行外的任何人，透露过目前开启保险库门那把锁所用的那组特定暗码？」

「没有，先生，当真没有；我这人再小心不过，对自己肩上这副担子的分量也感受得太深切了，断不至于不把这样要紧的秘密以最大的细心和戒备守着。」

===Original===
Mr. Sylvester's voice, careful as he was to modulate it, showed a secret discouragement. "The vaults then as far as you know, are safe when once they are closed for the night?"

"Yes sir." The janitor's face expressed a slight degree of wonder, but his voice was emphatic.

Mr. Sylvester's eye travelled in the direction of the screen. "Very well," said he; and paused to reflect.

In the interim the door opened for a second time. "A gentleman to see Mr. Stuyvesant," said a voice.

With an air of relief the director hastily rose, and before Mr. Sylvester had realized his position, left the room and closed the door behind him. A knell seemed to ring its note in Mr. Sylvester's breast. The janitor, released as he supposed from all constraint, stepped hastily forward.

===Chinese===
西尔维斯特先生的嗓音——尽管他小心翼翼地调节着——仍透露出一种隐秘的气馁。「那么，就你所知，保险库一旦夜里锁好，便是安全的？」

「是的，先生。」看门人脸上一度露出几分诧异之色，可答话的口吻是断然的。

西尔维斯特先生的目光朝屏风那边投去。「很好。」说着，他停下来沉吟。

就在这当口，门第二次开了。「有位先生要见斯泰弗森特先生。」一个声音报信道。

那位董事面露如释重负之色，匆忙起身，竟在西尔维斯特先生尚未及看清事态之前，便出了屋，随手把门带上。一声丧钟似的音调似乎在西尔维斯特先生胸口敲响。看门人——自以为已从一切约束中解脱出来——急忙跨步上前。

===Original===
"That box has been found unlocked," he cried with a wave of his hand towards the table; "someone has been to the vaults, and I—Oh, sir," he hurriedly exclaimed, disregarding in his agitation the stern and forbidding look which Mr. Sylvester in his secret despair had made haste to assume, "you did not want me to say anything about the time you came down so early in the morning, and I went out and left you alone in the bank, and you went to the vaults and opened Mr. Stuyvesant's box by mistake, with a toothpick as you remember?"

The mirror that looked down upon that pair, showed one very white face at that moment, but the screen that had trembled a moment before, stood strangely still in the silence.

"No," came at length from Mr. Sylvester, with a composure that astonished himself. "I was not questioning you about matters of a year agone. But you might have told that incident if you pleased; it was very easily explainable."

===Chinese===
「那只匣子被人发觉没上锁。」他嚷道，一只手朝桌上一挥，「有人到保险库去过，而我——噢，先生，」他急切地喊道，激动之中全然不顾西尔维斯特先生在隐秘绝望中急忙摆出的那副严厉拒人之色，「那回您一大清早下楼来，我出去、把您一个人留在银行里，您下了保险库，还用一根牙签把斯泰弗森特先生的匣子错打开了，您记起来了吧？您是不要我就这事多嘴的！」

俯视着这一双人的那面镜子，此刻映出了一张煞白的脸，可方才颤动过的那面屏风，在这一片寂静中却怪异得很——纹丝不动。

「不。」西尔维斯特先生终于开了口，那份镇定连他自己也为之诧异。「我并非在盘问你一年前那桩事。可你若愿意，原也可以把那件事说出来；那是极易解释清楚的。」

===Original===
"Yes sir, I know, and I beg pardon for alluding to it, but I was so taken aback, sir, by your questions; I wanted to tell the exact truth, and I did not want to say anything that would hurt you with Mr. Stuyvesant; that is if I could help it. I hope I did right, sir," he blundered on, conscious he was uttering words he might better have kept to himself, but too embarrassed to know how to emerge from the difficulty into which his mingled zeal and anxiety had betrayed him. "I was never a good hand at answering questions, and if anything really serious has happened, I shall wish you had taken me at my word and dismissed me immediately after that affair. Constantia Maria would have been a little worse off perhaps, but I should not be on hand to answer questions, and—"

"Hopgood!"

===Chinese===
「是的，先生，我知道，我提它一嘴还求您宽恕；可您那些问题着实把我吓了一跳，先生；我既想着一字不差地说出实话，又不愿说出什么于您在斯泰弗森特先生面前不利的话来——前提是我能不说便不说。但愿我没做错，先生。」他磕磕巴巴地往下说，明知自己正吐出几句本该烂在肚里的话，却窘迫得不知怎样才能从这份由热心与焦虑交织而成的难局里脱身。「我向来不善应对盘问，要是当真出了什么了不起的大事，我倒要盼着您当年那事之后便依着我所言把我辞退了。康斯坦蒂娅·玛丽亚（Constantia Maria）的处境或许要稍差一些，可我也不至于站在这里受人盘问，而且——」

「霍普古德！」

===Original===
The man started, eyed Mr. Sylvester's white but powerfully controlled countenance, seemed struck with something he saw there, and was silent.

"You make too much now, as you made too much then of a matter that having its sole ground in a mistake, is, as I say, easily explainable. This affair which has come up now, is not so clear. Three of the boxes have been opened, and from one certain valuables have been taken. Can you give me any information that will assist us in our search after the culprit?"

"No sir." The tone was quite humble, Hopgood drew back unconsciously towards the door.

"As for the mistake of a year ago to which you have seen proper to allude, I shall myself take pains to inform Mr. Stuyvesant of it, since it has made such an impression upon you that it trammels your honesty and makes you consider it at all necessary to be anxious about it at this time."

And Hopgood unused to sarcasm from those lips, drew himself together, and with one more agitated look at the box on the table, sidled awkwardly from the room.

===Chinese===
那人一惊，瞧了瞧西尔维斯特先生那张煞白却强自镇定的脸，似乎被所见之色触到了什么，便不再作声。

「您现在把这件事看得太重，正如您当年也把它看得太重——可这件事唯一的根由，原不过是一桩误会，如我所说，是极易解释清楚的。眼下冒出来的这桩事，便没那么明白了。三只匣子被人开过，其中一只少了若干值钱之物。你可有丝毫线索，能助我们追查那罪魁？」

「没有，先生。」口吻十分谦卑，霍普古德下意识朝门口退去。

「至于一年前那桩误会——你既觉得可以提及——我自会亲自费神告知斯泰弗森特先生；因为此事在你心上留下这般深的印象，竟至妨碍了你的诚实，叫你觉得此时此刻仍非为此忧心不可。」

霍普古德不习惯从那张嘴里听到挖苦之辞，便把身子一缩；再朝桌上那只匣子投去一道激动的一瞥，便侧着身子尴尬地退出了屋子。

===Original===
Mr. Sylvester at once advanced to the screen which he hastily pushed aside. "Well, sir," said he, meeting the detective's wavering eye and forcing him to return his look, "you have now seen the various employees of the bank and heard most of them converse. Is there anything more you would like to inquire into before giving us the opinion I requested?"

"No sir," said the detective, coming forward, but very slowly and somewhat hesitatingly for him. "I think I am ready to say—"

Here the door opened, and Mr. Stuyvesant returned. The detective drew a breath of relief and repeated his words with a businesslike assurance. "I think I am ready to say, that from the nature of the theft and the mysterious manner in which it has been perpetrated, suspicion undoubtedly points to someone connected with the bank. That is all that you require of me today?" he added, with a bow of some formality in the direction of Mr. Sylvester.

===Chinese===
西尔维斯特先生立刻走到屏风前，匆匆把它推到一边。「好啦，先生。」他说，迎上侦探那游移的目光，逼着对方回看他，「您现已见过行里的几位雇员，也听过他们大半的人开口。在作出我所求的那个判断之前，您还有什么要查问的吗？」

「没有了，先生。」侦探说着，走上前来——可对他而言，这一回却是慢得出奇，也略带迟疑。「我想我可以说了——」

正在这时，门开了，斯泰弗森特先生回来了。侦探松了一口气，以一种公事公办的笃定把自己方才的话再说一遍：「我想我可以这么说：从这桩窃案的性质、及其所作的神秘手段来看，疑点无疑指向行内某位与此银行有牵连之人。今日您要我做的，就这些？」他添了一句，朝西尔维斯特先生的方向略略鞠了一礼，带几分礼数。

===Original===
"Yes," was the short reply. But in an instant a change passed over the stately form of the speaker. Advancing to Mr. Gryce, he confronted him with a countenance almost majestic in its severity, and somewhat severely remarked, "This is a serious charge to bring against men whose countenances you yourself have denominated as honest. Are we to believe you have fully considered the question, and realize the importance of what you say?"

"Mr. Sylvester," replied the detective, with great self-possession and some dignity, "a man who is brought every day of his life into positions where the least turning of a hair will sink a man or save him, learns to weigh his words, before he speaks even in such informal inquiries as these."

Mr. Sylvester bowed and turned towards Mr. Stuyvesant. "Is there any further action you would like to have taken in regard to this matter today?" he asked, without a tremble in his voice.

With a glance at the half open box of the absent Mr. Harrington, the agitated director slowly shook his head. "We must have time to think," said he.

===Chinese===
「是的。」短短一句作答。可说话人那庄严的身影上立时掠过一丝变化。他朝格莱斯先生迈了一步，以一张严峻得近乎威仪的脸迎上他，略带严峻地说道：「您方才亲自断定这些人的面相诚实，如今却要对他们下这样一桩严重的指控。我们是否可以相信，您已把这个问题通盘思虑过，也明白您这番话的分量？」

「西尔维斯特先生，」侦探答道，自持之中带几分尊严，「一个人，若每日每夜都被置于那种境地——一丝头发的偏斜便能令一人沉沦或得救——这样的人，纵使在这般非正式的查询里，开口之前也学会了字字斟酌。」

西尔维斯特先生鞠了一躬，转向斯泰弗森特先生。「此事今日您还想有何进一步的举动么？」他问，嗓音分毫不颤。

那位激动的董事朝缺席的哈灵顿先生那只半开的匣子瞥了一眼，缓缓摇了摇头。「我们总得有些工夫来想一想。」他说。

===Original===
Mr. Gryce at once took up his hat. "If the charge implied in my opinion strikes you, gentlemen, as serious, you must at least acknowledge that your own judgment does not greatly differ from mine, or why such unnecessary agitation in regard to a loss so petty, by a gentleman worth as we are told his millions." And with this passing shot, to which neither of his auditors responded, he made his final obeisance and calmly left the room.

Mr. Sylvester and Mr. Stuyvesant slowly confronted one another.

"The man speaks the truth," said the former. "You at least suspect someone in the bank, Mr. Stuyvesant?"

"I have no wish to," hastily returned the other, "but facts—"

"Would facts of this nature have any weight with you against the unspotted character of a man never known by you to meditate, much less commit a dishonest action?"

"No; yet facts are facts, and if it is proved that someone in our employ has perpetrated a theft, the mind will unconsciously ask who, and remain uneasy till it is satisfied."

"And if it never is?"

"It will always ask who, I suppose."

===Chinese===
格莱斯先生立刻拿起帽子。「诸位先生，倘若我那意见所暗含的指控，在你们看来严重得很，那你们至少也得承认：你们自己的判断与我的也相去无几；否则，损失如此微末，又出自一位据说身家百万的先生——何苦这般不必要的激动？」这一记临别的冷箭，两位听者都没有接；他作了最后一礼，从容离屋。

西尔维斯特先生与斯泰弗森特先生缓缓相对而视。

「此人说的乃是实话。」前一位说道。「您至少是怀疑行里某个人的吧，斯泰弗森特先生？」

「我无意如此。」对方匆匆答道，「可事实——」

「这一类事实，与一个您从未见过其心萌歹念、更毋庸说行不诚实之事的人那清白无瑕的品格相权衡，在您这边当真有什么分量么？」

「没有；可事实终归是事实，倘若证明我们雇员中有人行窃，人心便会不自觉地追问是谁，不得到满足便不得安生。」

「可若始终不得满足呢？」

「我想它永远都会追问一个是谁。」

===Original===
Mr. Sylvester drew back. "The matter shall be pushed," said he; "you shall be satisfied. Surveillance over each man employed in this institution ought sooner or later to elicit the truth. The police shall take it in charge."

Mr. Stuyvesant looked uneasy. "I suppose it is only justice," murmured he, "but it is a scandal I would have been glad to avoid."

"And I, but circumstances admit of no other course. The innocent must not suffer for the guilty, even so far as an unfounded suspicion would lead."

"No, no, of course not." And the director bustled about after his overcoat and hat.

Mr. Sylvester watched him with growing sadness. "Mr. Stuyvesant," said he, as the latter stood before him ready for the street, "we have always been on terms of friendship, and nothing but the most pleasant relations have ever existed between us. Will you pardon me if I ask you to give me your hand in good day?"

The director paused, looked a trifle astonished, but held out his hand not only with cordiality but very evident affection.

"Good day," cried he, "good day."

===Chinese===
西尔维斯特先生退后一步。「此事定要追查到底。」他说，「您总会得到满足。对这机构里每一名雇员的监视，迟早会逼出真相。警察局来接手吧。」

斯泰弗森特先生面有难色。「我想这也不过是公道。」他低声道，「可这是一桩丑闻，我原是极愿避开的。」

「我也是，可眼下的情势不容别种做法。无辜者不可代人受过——哪怕只是一个毫无根据的疑心所致的那一点点。」

「那是，那是，自然。」那位董事忙忙地张罗起自己的外套和礼帽。

西尔维斯特先生目送他，神情越发哀戚。「斯泰弗森特先生，」当对方已穿戴整齐、立在他面前预备上街时，他开口道，「你我向来交情深厚，彼此之间除了最为融洽的情谊，再无别物。你能否恕我冒昧——临别之际，与你握一握手，道一声好走？」

那位董事一怔，似有几分诧异，可伸出手来时，不仅热忱，还带着显而易见的情谊。

「好走，」他喊道，「好走。」

===Original===
Mr. Sylvester pressed that hand, and then with a dignified bow, allowed the director to depart. It was his last effort at composure. When the door closed, his head sank on his hands, and life with all its hopes and honors, love and happiness, seemed to die within him.

He was interrupted at length by Bertram. "Well, uncle?" asked the young man with unrestrained emotion.

"The theft has been committed by someone in this bank; so the detective gives out, and so we are called upon to believe. *Who* the man is who has caused us all this misery, neither he, nor you, nor I, nor anyone, is likely to very soon determine. Meantime—"

"Well?" cried Bertram anxiously, after a moment of suspense.

"Meantime, courage!" his uncle resumed with forced cheerfulness.

===Chinese===
西尔维斯特先生紧了紧那只手，随即以一礼相送，让那位董事走了。这是他镇定自持的最后一番努力。门一关上，他的头便颓然垂落到双手之上，生命——连同它一切的希望与荣光、爱与幸福——似乎都在他心里枯死了。

最终打断他的，是伯特兰。「怎么样，叔父？」那年轻人毫不掩饰情感地问。

「这桩窃案是行里某个人作的；侦探是这么说的，我们也被迫照此相信。至于*那个*给我们招来这许多苦恼的人，究竟是谁——他也好，你也好，我也好，再或者旁人也好——只怕谁也不能很快断定。眼下——」

「眼下怎样？」伯特兰在一阵悬念之后焦急地喊道。

「眼下——鼓起勇气罢！」叔父强作轻快地接道。

===Original===
But as he was leaving the bank he came up to Bertram, and laying his hand on his shoulder, quietly said:

"I want you to go immediately to my house upon leaving here. I may not be back till midnight, and Miss Fairchild may need the comfort of your presence. Will you do it, Bertram?"

"Uncle! I—"

"Hush! you will comfort me best by doing what I ask. May I rely upon you?"

"Always."

"That is enough."

And with just a final look, the two gentlemen parted, and the shadow which had rested all day upon the bank, deepened over Bertram's head like a pall.

It was not lifted by the sight of Hopgood stealing a few minutes later towards the door by which his uncle had departed, his face pale, and his eyes fixed in a stare, that bespoke some deep and moving determination.

===Chinese===
可临离开银行之际，他走到伯特兰跟前，把一只手搭在侄儿肩上，轻声道：

「我要你一离开此地，便立即到我宅子里去。我也许到半夜都回不来，费尔柴尔德小姐（Miss Fairchild）说不定需要你陪伴、得些安慰。你可愿意，伯特兰？」

「叔父！我——」

「嘘！你依我所求去做，便是给我最大的宽慰了。我能指望你么？」

「永远能。」

「这就够了。」

两位先生彼此投去最后一眼，便作别了；那一整日笼罩在银行之上的阴影，此刻如同一件裹尸的寿衣，在伯特兰头顶越压越低。

几分钟之后，他又瞥见霍普古德悄然朝叔父离去的那扇门溜去——脸白如纸，一双眼睛定定地瞪着，那瞪视里透出某种深切而撼人的决心——这阴影并未因此消减分毫。

## XXIII The Poem / 二十三 诗

===Original===
> "I've shot my arrow o'er the house

 And hurt my brother."

When Miss Belinda first saw Paula, she did not, like her sister, remark upon the elegance of her appearance, the growth of her beauty, or the evidences of increased refinement in the expression of her countenance and the carriage of her form, but with her usual penetration noted simply, the sadness in her eye and the tremulous motion of her lip.
"You had then become fond of your cousin?" queried she with characteristic bluntness.
Paula not understanding the motive of this remark, questioned her with a look.
"Young faces do not grow pale or bright eyes become troubled without a cause. Grief for your cousin might explain it, but if you have suffered from no grief—"
"My cousin was very kind to me," hurriedly interrupted Paula. "Her death was very sudden and very heartrending."
"So it was;" returned Miss Belinda, "and I expected to see you look worn and sad but not restless and feverish. You have a living grief, Paula, what is it?"
The young girl started and looked down. For the first time in her life she wished to avoid that penetrating glance. "If I have, I cannot talk of it," she murmured. "I have experienced so much this past week; my coming away was so unexpected, that I hardly understand my own feelings, or realize just what it is that troubles me most. All that I know is, that I am very tired and so sad, it seems as if the sun would never shine again."
"There is then something you have not written me?" inquired the inexorable Miss Belinda.
"The experiences of this last week could never be written—or told," returned Paula with a droop of her head. "Upon some things our better wisdom places a stone which only the angels can roll away. The future lies all open before us; do not let us disturb the past."
And Miss Belinda was forced to be content lest she should seem to be over anxious.

===Chinese===
> 「我把箭射过了屋脊，
> 却伤了我的兄弟。」

贝琳达小姐初见宝拉时，并不像她姐姐那样，称道她仪态的雅致、容颜的愈发秀美，也不像她那样，称道她眉目神情与举止身段间日益流露出来的教养痕迹；她凭着素来那份洞察之力，单只注意到了她眼中的那一份哀愁，以及嘴唇那抑制不住的轻颤。
「那么，你是已经喜欢上你的表姐了？」她以她那惯有的直截了当问道。
宝拉不明白这话用意何在，只拿一道目光去探问。
「年轻的脸不会无缘无故地失了血色，明亮的眼睛也不会无缘无故地蒙上愁云。为你的表姐伤心，原可解释这一切；可你若不是为此而苦——」
「表姐待我极好。」宝拉急忙打断道，「她的死来得那样突然，又那样叫人心碎。」
「正是，」贝琳达小姐答道，「我也料到你会面容憔悴、神色凄楚，却没料到你会这般心神不宁、躁急如火。你有一桩眼前正熬着的忧愁，宝拉，是什么？」
少女猛地一惊，垂下了眼。这是她平生头一回想避开那洞察一切的目光。「就算有，我也说不上来。」她低声说，「这一周里我经历了太多；我之离开又来得那样出乎意料，以致我自己也摸不清我自己的心情，弄不明白究竟是什么最搅扰着我。我所知道的，不过是我累极了，又悲伤极了，仿佛太阳再也不会照临了似的。」
「那么，你有事瞒着没写信告诉我？」不肯通融的贝琳达小姐追问。
「这一周的经历，是写不出来——也讲不出来的。」宝拉垂着头答道，「有些事，我们更深的智慧会在其上压下一块石头，唯有天使才能将它滚开。未来正一片开阔地展现在我们前头；我们莫去惊扰过去罢。」
贝琳达小姐也只得就此满足，免得显出自己过于焦虑。

===Original===
Not so the various neighbors and friends to whom the lengthened sojourn of one of their number in an atmosphere of such wealth and splendor, possessed something of the charm of a forbidden romance. For months Paula was obliged to endure questions, that it required all her self-control to answer with calmness and propriety. But at length the most insatiable gossip amongst them was satisfied; Paula's figure was no longer a novelty in their streets; curiosity languished and the young girl was allowed to rest.

===Chinese===
邻里亲友却不是这样。他们当中有一个人，竟在那般富丽华贵的氛围里盘桓了那许久，于他们便颇有一种被禁的传奇故事般的诱惑。一连好几个月，宝拉不得不忍受种种盘问，须得拿出全部的涵养，才能不失平静、不失得体地一一作答。可到末了，连他们当中最爱打听的人也终于餍足了；宝拉的身影在他们街市上已不再算件新鲜事；好奇心也渐渐委顿下去，这个少女这才得以休歇。

===Original===
And now could those who loved her, discern that with the lapse of time and the daily breathings of her native air, the sad white look had faded from her face, leaving it a marvel of freshness and positive, if somewhat spiritualized, beauty. The print of deeper thoughts and holier yearnings was there, but no sign of blighted hopes or uncomprehended passions. A passing wind had blown the froth from off the cup, but had not disturbed the sparkle of the wine. She had looked in the face of grief, but had not as yet been clasped in her relentless arms. Only two things could vitally disturb her; a letter from Cicely, or a sudden meeting in the village streets with that elderly lady who haunted the Japha mansion. The former because it recalled a life around which her fancies still played with dangerous persistency, and the latter because it aroused vain and inexplicable conjectures as to that person's strange and lingering look in her direction. Otherwise she was happy; finding in this simple village-life a meaning and a purpose which her short but passionate outlook on a broader field, had taught her, perhaps, both to detect and comprehend. She no longer walked solitary with nature. The woods, the mountains with all their varying panoply of exuberant verdure, had acquired a human significance. At her side went the memories of beloved faces, the thoughts of trusted friends. From the clouds looked forth a living eye, and in the sound of rustling leaf and singing streamlet, spake the voices of human longing and human joy.

===Chinese===
到了这时，爱她的人才能看出：随着日复一日、故土空气的吹拂，那张脸上的凄白愁容已渐褪去，留下一种清新得令人赞叹的、实实在在的——纵也略带几分空灵的——美。更深沉的思想、更圣洁的向往所印下的痕迹尚在，却不见有什么破灭的希望、什么无从索解的激情的影子。一阵过路的风把杯口的浮沫吹去了，却没有搅扰那酒的光华。她曾与忧愁照过面，却尚未被她那无情的双臂紧紧搂住。只有两件事还能当真搅动她的心：一封西塞莉的来信，或在村中街上一时撞见那位盘桓在雅法（Japha）旧宅的老夫人。前者是因为它唤回了一段生活，而她的遐思至今仍以一种危险的执拗在那段生活上盘桓不去；后者是因为那人投向她那个方向的那种古怪而缠绵的目光，每每惹起她种种徒然的、难以索解的揣度。除此之外，她是快活的；她在这质朴的村居岁月里，寻得了一种意味、一种旨趣，而这，或许是她在一片更广阔的天地间那短促却热烈的远望，已教她既能识得、也能领会的了。她不再孤零零地独自与自然同行。那林木、那山峦——连同它们那变幻无穷、葱茏丰茂的全副盛装——已带上了一种人事的意味。走在她身畔的，是挚爱容颜的回忆，是良朋益友的思念。云间有一只活的眼向下张望；在飒飒叶声与潺潺溪响之间，诉说的，正是人间的渴慕与人间的欢悦。

===Original===
Her aunts had explained their position to Paula and she had responded by expressing her determination to be a teacher. But they would not hear of that at present, and while she waited their pleasure in the matter, she did what she could to assist them in their simple home-life and daily duties, lending her beauty to tasks that would have made the eyes of some of her quondam admirers open with surprise, if only they could have followed the action of her hands, after having once caught a glimpse of the face that brightened above them. And so the summer months went by and September came.

===Chinese===
两位姨母已向宝拉说明了自己的境况，宝拉的回应是表明了自己要做一名教师的决心。可她们当下不肯依。在她等候她们就此拿主意的那段日子里，她尽其所能地，帮着她们操持那简单的家计和日常的活计，把那份容貌也借给那些活计去——那些活计，倘若她从前的几位爱慕者，只消瞥见那双在这些活计上头亮起来的脸，便能跟踪这双手的一举一动，定要叫他们看得瞠目结舌。夏季的几个月就这样过去，九月来了。

===Original===
There was to be an entertainment in the village and Paula was to assist. The idea had come from her aunt and was not to be rejected. In one of the strange incomprehensible moods which sometimes came upon her at this time, she had written a poem, and nothing would do but that she must read it before the assembled company of neighbors and friends, that were to be gathered at the Squire's house on this gala evening. She did not wish to do it. The sacred sense of possession passes when we uncover our treasure to another's eyes, giving way to a lower feeling not to be courted by one of Paula's sensitive nature. Besides she would rather have poured this first outburst of secret enthusiasm into other ears than these; but she had given her word and the ordeal must be submitted to. There are many who remember how she looked on that night. She had arrayed herself for the occasion, in the prettiest of her dresses, and mindful of Ona's injunction, did not mar the effect of its soft and uniform gray with any hint of extraneous color. The result was that they saw only her beauty; and what beauty! A very old man, an early settler in the village, who had tottered out to enjoy a last glimpse of life before turning his aged face to the wall, said it made the thought of heaven a little more real. "I can go home and think how the angels look," said he in his simple, half-childish way. And no one contradicted him, for there was a still light on her face that was less of earth than heaven, though why it should rest there tonight she least of all could have told, for her poem had to do with earth and its deepest passions and its wildest unrest. It was a clarion blast, not a dreaming rhapsody, that lay coiled up in the paper she held in her hand.

===Chinese===
村里要办一场游艺会，宝拉也得出一份力。这主意是她姨母出的，推辞不得。正逢她这时常发作的那种古怪而难以言说的情绪之一，她写了一首诗，而当下便非得当着那一晚齐聚在乡绅（Squire）家的邻里亲友的面，亲自把它朗诵出来不可。她本不愿做这事。那神圣的、独自拥有的感觉，一旦我们将自己的珍藏袒露在别人眼前，便已逝去，让位于一种低一等的情绪——这种情绪，以宝拉那敏感的性情，是断不肯招惹的。况且，她这一股头一次迸发的隐秘热忱，她本宁愿倾注在别的一些耳朵里，而不愿倾注在这些耳朵里；可她既已应承下，这场苦役便非熬过去不可。那一晚她是什么模样，至今仍有许多人记得。她为这事特意拣了自己最漂亮的那一身衣裙穿上，又记着奥娜（Ona）的叮嘱，不让任何一点旁的色彩来损那一身柔和、纯一的灰色。结果便是，他们眼中只见她的美；那是何等的美啊！村里一位极年老的、最早的一批住户，已是颤颤巍巍地摸出来，想在把那张老脸转向墙壁、撒手之前，再瞧这人生最后一眼，他说这一瞧，倒叫那「天堂」的念头实在了几分。「我能回家了，」他半孩子气、极朴实地说，「能回家去想想天使是什么模样了。」无人驳他，因为她脸上有一脉静静的光，那光里属地的少，属天的多，至于它今夜为何偏偏落在她脸上，她自己比谁都说不清，因为她那首诗所关涉的，原是这大地，是这大地最深的激情、最狂躁的不安。盘在她手心里那张纸上的，是一声号角，而非一场梦中的狂想。

===Original===
My readers must pardon me if I give them Paula's poem, for without it they would not understand its effect and consequent result. It was called, *The Defence of the Bride*, and was of the old ballad order. As she rose to read, many of the younger ones in the audience began cautiously to move to one side, but at the first words, young as well as old paused and listened where they stood, for her voice was round and full, and the memory of clashing spears and whirling battle-axes that informed the war-song which she had heard Bertram play, was with her, to give color to her tones and fire to her glance.

===Chinese===
读者诸君还请见恕，我这里不得不把宝拉那首诗也录出来，否则他们便无从领会它的效果及其后所引出的种种。这首诗题为《新娘的护卫》（*The Defence of the Bride*），是仿古歌谣一脉。她起身诵读之时，听众里那些年纪轻的有好几位，便开始小心翼翼地朝一旁挪动，可她那头几句一出口，老少一齐顿住了脚，就地听了起来；原来她嗓音圆润饱满，而她曾听伯特兰弹过的那支战歌——长矛相击、战斧飞舞的种种记忆便贯注其间——此刻也在她心里，为她的声调添上色彩，为她的目光点燃火光。

===Original===
> He was coming from the altar when the tocsin rang alarm,

 With his fair young wife beside him, lovely in her bridal charm;
 But he was not one to palter with a duty, or to slight
 The trumpet-call of honor for his vantage or delight.
> Turning from the bride beside him to his stern and martial train,
 From their midst he summoned to him the brothers of Germain;
 At the word they stepped before him, nine strong warriors brave and true,
 From the youngest to the eldest, Enguerrand to mighty Hugh.
> "Sons of Germain, to your keeping do I yield my bride today.
 Guard her well as you do love me; guard her well and holily.
 Dearer than mine own soul to me, you will hold her as your life,
 'Gainst the guile of seeming friendship and the force of open strife."
> "We will guard her," cried they firmly; and with just another glance
 On the yearning and despairing in his young wife's countenance,
 Gallant Beaufort strode before them down the aisle and through the door,
 And a shadow came and lingered where the sunlight stood before.
> Eight long months the young wife waited, watching from her bridal room
 For the coming of her husband up the valley forest's gloom.
 Eight long months the sons of Germain paced the ramparts and the wall,
 With their hands upon their halberds ready for the battle-call.
> Then there came a sound of trumpets pealing up the vale below,
 And a dozen floating banners lit the forest with their glow,
 And the bride arose like morning when it feels the sunlight nigh,
 And her smile was like a rainbow flashing from a misty sky.
> But the eldest son of Germain lifting voice from off the wall,
 Cried aloud, "It is a stranger's and not Sir Beaufort's call;
 Have you ne'er a slighted lover or a kinsman with a heart
 Base enough to seek his vengeance at the sharp end of the dart?"
> "There is Sassard of the Mountains," answered she without guile,
 "While I wedded at the chancel, he stood mocking in the aisle;
 And my maidens say he swore there that for all my plighted vow,
 They would see me in his castle yet upon Morency's brow."
> "It is Sassard and no other then," her noble guardian cried;
 "There is craft in yonder summons," and he rung his sword beside.
 "To the walls, ye sons of Germain! and as each would hold his life
 From the bitter shame of falsehood, let us hold our master's wife."
> "Can you hold her, can you shield her from the breezes that await?"
 Cried the stinging voice of Sassard from his stand beside the gate.
 "If you have the power to shield her from the sunlight and the wind,
 You may shield her from stern Sassard when his falchion is untwined."
> "We can hold her, we can shield her," leaped like fire from off the wall,
 And young Enguerrand the valiant, sprang out before them all.
 "And if breezes bring dishonor, we will guard her from their breath,
 Though we yield her to the keeping of the sacred arms of Death."
> And with force that never faltered, did they guard her all that day,
 Though the strength of triple armies seemed to battle in the fray,
 The old castle's rugged ramparts holding firm against the foe,
 As a goodly dyke resisteth the whelming billow's flow.
> But next morning as the sunlight rose in splendor over all,
 Hugh the mighty, sank heart-wounded in his station on the wall,
 At the noon the valiant Raoul of the merry eye and heart,
 Gave his beauty and his jestings to the foeman's jealous dart.
> Gallant Maurice next sank faltering with a death wound 'neath his hair,
 But still fighting on till Sassard pressed across him up the stair.
 Generous Clement followed after, crying as his spirit passed,
 "Sons of Germain to the rescue, and be loyal to the last!"
> Gentle Jaspar, lordly Clarence, Sessamine the doughty brand,
 Even Henri who had yielded ne'er before to mortal hand;
 One by one they fall and perish, while the vaunting foemen pour
 Through the breach and up the courtway to the very turret's door.
> Enguerrand and Stephen only now were left of all that nine,
 To protect the single stairway from the traitor's fell design;
 But with might as 'twere of thirty, did they wield the axe and brand,
 Striving in their desperation the fierce onslaught to withstand.
> But what man of power so godlike he can stay the billow's wrack,
 Or with single-handed weapon hold an hundred foemen back!
 As the sun turned sadly westward, with a wild despairing cry,
 Stephen bowed his noble forehead and sank down on earth to die.
> "Ah ha!" then cried cruel Sassard with his foot upon the stair,
 "Have I come to thee, my boaster?" and he whirled his sword in air.
 "Thou who pratest of thy power to protect her to the death,
 What think'st thou now of Sassard and the wind's aspiring breath?"
> "What I think let this same show you," answered fiery Enguerrand,
 And he poised his lofty battle-ax with sure and steady hand;
 "Now as Heaven loveth justice, may this deathly weapon fall
 On the murderer of my brothers and th' undoer of us all."
> With one mighty whirl he sent it; flashing from his hand it came,
 Like the lightning from the heavens in a whirl of awful flame,
 And betwixt the brows of Sassard and his two false eyeballs passed,
 And the murderer sank before it, like a tree before the blast.
> "Now ye minions of a traitor if you look for vengeance, come!"
 And his voice was like a trumpet when it clangs a victor home.
 But a cry from far below him rose like thunder upward, "Nay!
 Let them turn and meet the *husband* if they hunger for the fray."
> O the yell that sprang to heaven as that voice swept up the stair,
 And the slaughter dire that followed in another moment there!
 From the least unto the greatest, from the henchman to the lord,
 Not a man on all that stairway lived to sheath again his sword.
> At the top that flame-bound forehead, at the base that blade of fire—
 'Twas the meeting of two tempests in their potency and ire.
 Ere the moon could falter inward with its pity and its woe,
 Beaufort saw the path before him unencumbered of the foe.
> Saw his pathway unencumbered and strode up and o'er the floor,
 Even to the very threshold of his lovely lady's door,
 And already in his fancy did he see the golden beam
 Of her locks upon his shoulder and her sweet eyes' happy gleam:
> When behold a form upstarting from the shadows at his side.
 That with naked sword uplifted barred the passage to his bride;
 It was Enguerrand the dauntless, but with staring eyes and hair
 Blowing wild about a forehead pale as snow in moonlit glare.
> "Ah my master, we have held her, we have guarded her," he said,
 "Not a shadow of dishonor has so much as touched her head.
 Twenty wretches lie below there with the brothers of Germain,
 Twenty foemen of her honor that I, Enguerrand, have slain.
> "But one other foe remaineth, one remaineth yet," he cried,
 "Which it fits this hand to punish ere you cross unto your bride.
 It is I, Enguerrand!" shrieked he; "and as I have slain the rest,
 So I smite this foeman also!"—and his sword plunged through his breast.
> O the horror of that moment! "Art thou mad my Enguerrand?"
 Cried his master, striving wildly to withdraw the fatal brand.
 But the stern youth smiling sadly, started back from his embrace,
 While a flash like summer lightning, flickered direful on his face.
> "Yes, a traitor worse than Sassard;" and he pointed down the stair,
 "For my heart has dared to love her whom my hand defended there.
 While the others fought for honor, I by passion was made strong,
 Set your heel upon my bosom for my soul has done you wrong.
> "But," and here he swayed and faltered till his knee sank on the floor,
 Yet in falling turned his forehead ever toward that silent door;
 "But your warrior hand my master, may take mine without a stain,
 For my hand has e'er been loyal, and your enemy is slain."

===Chinese===
> 他正从祭坛前走来，警钟忽鸣示警，
> 身畔是他年轻美貌的妻子，新嫁娘的娇艳可亲；
> 然而他绝非那等玩忽职责之辈，亦不肯为
> 一己之便、一时之欢，而轻慢荣誉的号声。
> 他撇下身畔的新娘，转向那一列肃杀的甲士，
> 从中点唤日耳曼（Germain）家的众兄弟上前；
> 一声令下，他们便步到他跟前，九位壮士，既勇且义，
> 自最幼的昂盖兰（Enguerrand），至最雄强的休（Hugh）。
> 「日耳曼的儿子们，今日我将新娘托付于你们。
> 你们若爱我，便好生护持她；当以圣洁之心护持她。
> 她于我比自己的灵魂更亲，你们当视她如自己的性命，
> 挡住那似友实敌的诡诈，挡住那明火执仗的强攻。」
> 「我们定当护持她。」他们毅然呼道；博福尔（Beaufort）爵士
> 仅仅又向那年轻妻子脸上殷殷绝望的神情投去一瞥，
> 便昂然走在他们前头，步下过道，跨出大门，
> 一片阴影便挪来停驻，在原是阳光立足的地方。
> 整整八个月，年轻的妻子守在新房里翘首，
> 只盼丈夫能从那林木阴翳的谷中走上前来。
> 整整八个月，日耳曼的儿子们在城头城墙上巡行，
> 手按戟柄，随时听候那一场厮杀的呼召。
> 忽而一阵号角之声，从下方谷中嘹亮地传上，
> 十余面飘扬的旗帜，以它们的光华点亮了山林，
> 新娘如觉到日光照临的晨光一般，霍然立起，
> 她的笑靥，恰如雾空里一闪而过的彩虹。
> 然日耳曼的长子，从城头扬声唤道：
> 「这一声号，乃是外人的号，并非博福尔爵士的号；
> 你们可有一位失意的旧情郎，或是一位亲人，
> 心肠卑鄙到要在箭镞的尖头上寻他的仇？」
> 「山中的萨萨尔（Sassard）便是一位。」她毫无机心地答道，
> 「我在圣坛前行礼之时，他便立在过道里讥诮；
> 我的侍女们说，他当众立过誓：任凭我已许下婚约，
> 终有一日要见我坐上他的城堡，在莫朗西（Morency）的山头。」
> 「那便是萨萨尔，再无别人。」她那高贵的守护人呼道；
> 「这一通召降里藏着诡诈。」说着他在身旁将剑振得铮然。
> 「上城来罢，日耳曼的儿子们！你们各人若要使自己
> 免遭背信失义那般苦楚的羞辱，便让我们一同守住主公之妻。」
> 「你们守得住她么，你们护得了她么，能挡得住即将到来的风？」
> 萨萨尔尖刻的嗓音，从他立在门畔的立处叫了下来。
> 「你们若有力将她从日头和风里护住，
> 或可从铁石心肠的萨萨尔手里，在他那把弯刀出鞘之时，也护得住她。」
> 「我们守得住，我们护得了。」这话如一道火光从城头迸出，
> 年轻而英勇的昂盖兰一跃而出，立在众人之前。
> 「纵然风里带来羞辱，我们也要挡住它的气息，
> 哪怕终须将她交到那神圣的死神怀抱之中。」
> 他们以从不退缩之力，那一整日将她死死守住，
> 纵使那敌阵仿佛集三军之力于这一场鏖战，
> 那古堡粗砺的城堞，仍死死抵住来犯之敌，
> 如同一道完好的堤堰，抵住那滔天巨浪的奔涌。
> 然而次日清晨，日头辉光万丈地升起之时，
> 雄强的休却在城头的岗位上，一伤心重之创而倒了下去；
> 到了正午，那眼波灵动、心性快活的勇者拉乌尔（Raoul），
> 把他的俊美与他的诙谐，一并给了敌人妒恨的飞镝。
> 英勇的莫里斯（Maurice）随后也踉跄着倒下，鬓发之下是致命一伤，
> 却仍厮杀不止，直到萨萨尔踏过他身上，奔上楼去。
> 慷慨的克莱门（Clement）紧随其后，在魂魄离身之时高呼：
> 「日耳曼的儿子们，速来救援，要忠贞到最后一刻！」
> 温文的雅斯帕（Jaspar），雍容的克拉伦斯（Clarence），持一把利剑的塞萨敏（Sessamine），
> 乃至那从未败于任何凡人之手的亨利（Henri）；
> 他们一个接一个倒下、殒命，而那喧嚷的敌军
> 一路穿过缺口，涌过庭院，直至塔楼的门下。
> 九人之中，如今只剩下昂盖兰与司蒂文（Stephen），
> 守住那唯一的楼梯，不让奸人凶残的奸计得逞；
> 然而他们挥动斧与剑，那一身气力竟如三十人一般，
> 拼着必死之心，要抵住那一场猛烈的攻扑。
> 然而哪有那般神勇之人，能遏住滔滔巨浪的肆虐，
> 或以一人一器之力，挡住上百名来敌！
> 日头凄然西斜之时，司蒂文发一声绝望的狂呼，
> 低下了他高贵的额角，倒在地上，气绝而亡。
> 「啊哈！」残忍的萨萨尔一脚已踏在楼梯之上，叫道，
> 「我寻到你了罢，我的夸口之人？」他将剑在空中一旋。
> 「你口口声声说你有护她到底之力，
> 如今你可怎样看待萨萨尔，看待那长风奔涌的喘息？」
> 「我所想的，便让这一下告诉你。」性如烈火的昂盖兰答道，
> 他以沉稳之手，将那一柄高高的战斧端端正正地举起；
> 「如今，上天既爱公义，愿这件杀伐之器
> 便落在那杀我众兄弟、覆我全族之人的身上。」
> 他猛然一旋，将那斧掷出；它从他手中飞出时寒光一道，
> 如雷霆从九天之上，在一团可怖的火焰中劈下，
> 自萨萨尔两眉之间、那两只奸诈的眼珠之间穿过去，
> 那杀人者便如一棵树被狂风拦腰折断，扑地而倒。
> 「奸贼的爪牙们，你们若要寻仇，便上来罢！」
> 他的嗓音如号角一般，将一名得胜者吹送回家。
> 然而脚下深处一声呼喊，如雷霆般滚滚而上：「且慢！
> 让他们掉头去会那位*丈夫*罢，倘若他们当真馋这场厮杀。」
> 哎呀，那一声随着嗓音卷上楼梯而冲上九天的嚎叫，
> 紧接着一刹那间，在那上面所爆发的那场可怖的屠戮！
> 自最微末的至最尊贵的，自家丁至主公，
> 那道楼梯上的所有人，没有一个还活着，能再度收剑入鞘。
> 在那顶端，那被火光缭绕的额角；在那底端，那道烈焰般的剑刃——
> 这是两场暴风雨，以它们的全部神威与全部怒火，撞在一处。
> 月轮尚不及带着它的怜悯与悲凄，向里头颤一颤光华，
> 博福尔已见他面前的去路，再无一敌可阻。
> 他见去路已通，便大步跨上那层楼板，
> 径直走到他那位娇美夫人的门前，
> 那一时，他幻梦之中，已仿佛看见
> 她金色的发缕搭上他的肩头，看见她那一双明眸里欢喜的光芒：
> 岂料一道身影从他身畔阴影里霍然跃起，
> 手举一柄出鞘的剑，拦在他去见新娘的路上；
> 那是英勇无惧的昂盖兰，可他双目圆睁，
> 头发在那月光惨照、白如雪的额角四下狂飞。
> 「啊，我的主公，我们守住了她，我们护住了她。」他说，
> 「半点玷污她的阴影，都不曾沾到她的头顶。
> 楼下躺着二十个恶徒，与日耳曼的众兄弟同卧一处，
> 那是二十个与她清白为敌之人，是我，昂盖兰，亲手斩却。
> 「可还有一个敌人留下，还有一个未曾了结。」他呼道，
> 「这一位，正当由这只手来惩治，在您跨去见新娘之前。
> 那便是我，昂盖兰！」他厉声叫道；「我既已杀却其余，
> 也当将这一位敌人一并斩却！」——一剑便刺入了自己的胸膛。
> 哎呀，那一刹那的可怖！「你疯了么，我的昂盖兰？」
> 他的主公狂乱地呼喊，拼命要把那把夺命的剑拔出。
> 然而那坚毅的青年含着一缕悲凄的笑，从他怀里往后一退，
> 一抹如夏日闪电般的光，在他脸上凄厉地一闪。
> 「不错，比萨萨尔更奸的叛徒；」他朝楼梯下一指，
> 「因为我的心，竟敢爱上我那只手所护卫着的人。
> 旁人皆为荣誉而战，我却因这一腔痴情而力大无穷，
> 请您一脚踏上我的胸膛罢，因为我的灵魂已对您不起。
> 「只是，」说到这里他身形一晃，踉跄着，直到一膝跪倒在地，
> 然而倒下之时，那额角仍始终朝着那一扇静默的门；
> 「只是，我的主公，您那战士之手，尽可取去我这一只手，而不带半点污名，
> 因为我这一只手向来忠贞，而您的敌人，已然伏诛。」

===Original===
A short silence followed the last word, then a burst of applause testified to the appreciation of her audience, and Paula crept away to hide her blushing cheeks in the comparative darkness of a little vine-covered balcony that jutted out from the anteroom. What were her thoughts as she leaned there! In the subsidence of any great emotion—and Paula had felt every word she uttered—there is more or less of shock and tumult. She did not think, she only felt. Suddenly a hand was laid on her arm and a low voice whispered in her ear,
"Did you write that poem yourself?"
Turning, she encountered the shadowy form of a woman leaning close at her side and appearing in the dim light that shone on her from the lamps beyond, an eager image of expectancy.
"Yes," returned Paula, "why do you ask?"
The woman, whoever she was, did not answer. "And you believe in such devotion as that!" she murmured. "You can understand a man, aye, or a woman either, risking happiness and fame, life and death, for the sake of a trust! Such things are not folly to you! You could see a heart spill itself drop by drop through a longer vigil than the eight months watching on the ramparts, and not sneer at a fidelity that could not falter because it had given its word? Speak; you write of faithfulness with a pen of fire, is your heart faithful too?"

===Chinese===
末了一个字落下，四下里静了片刻，随即一阵掌声骤起，可见她的听众是如何赏识她。宝拉悄悄地溜了开去，把两颊涨红的脸，藏到前厅外头那座爬满藤蔓的小阳台那一片相对幽暗的所在。她倚在那儿，心里翻腾着些什么啊！凡大悲大恸平复下来之际——宝拉方才每一个字都是感同身受念出来的——心头总免不了有些震荡与纷乱。她并不思考，她只是感觉。忽然一只手搭上了她的胳膊，一个低低的嗓音在她耳边低语：
「那首诗是你自己写的么？」
她一转身，正撞见一个女人的身影紧贴在她身侧，在那边灯盏投射过来的昏暗光线里，那身影现出一副殷切期待的急切模样。
「是的，」宝拉答道，「你为何这样问？」
那女人——无论她是谁——并不作答。「那么，你是相信世上有那般赤诚的！」她低声道，「你能明白，一个人，男人也罢，女人也罢，为着一桩所托，竟肯拿幸福与声名、拿生死去冒险！在你看来，那并非痴愚！你能看着一颗心，在比城头八个月的守望更久的守候里，一滴一滴地把自己沥尽，而不会去嗤笑那一份只因已许下诺言便再不肯动摇的忠贞？你说呀；你以一支火一般的笔来歌咏忠贞，那么你的心，可是也忠贞的？」

===Original===
There was something in these words, spoken as they were in a tone of suppressed passion, that startled and aroused Paula. Leaning forward, she endeavored to see the face of the woman who thus forcibly addressed her, but the light was too dim. The outline of a brow covered by some close headgear was all she could detect.
"You speak earnestly," said Paula, "but that is what I like. Fidelity to a cause, or fidelity to a trust, demands the sympathy and admiration of all honest and generous hearts. If I am ever called upon to maintain either, I hope that my enthusiasm will not have all been expended in words."
"You please me," murmured the woman, "you please me; will you come and see me and let me tell you a story to mate the poem you have given us tonight?"
The trembling eagerness of her tone it would be impossible to describe. Paula was thrilled by it. "If you will tell me who you are," said Paula, "I certainly will try and come. I should be glad to hear anything you have to relate to me."
"I thought everyone knew who I was," returned the woman; and drawing Paula back into the anteroom, she turned her face upon her. "Anyone will tell you where Margery Hamlin lives," said she. "Do not disappoint me, and do not keep me waiting long." And with a nod and a deep strange smile that made her aged face almost youthful, she entered the crowd and disappeared from Paula's sight.

===Chinese===
这话里——又是以那种压抑着激切的声调说出来的——颇有某种东西，叫宝拉既惊且动。她往前探了探身，想看清这个如此强有力地向她搭话的女人的脸，可光线实在太暗。她所能辨认的，不过是一道额角的轮廓，上头罩着一顶紧紧的头巾之类的物事。
「你说得恳切，」宝拉说，「我正喜欢这个。对一桩事业的忠贞，或对一桩所托的忠贞，原该唤起一切正直慷慨之心的同情与钦慕。倘若有一日，我竟被唤去要为这两者之中的任一个出力，我希望我的那一腔热忱，不至于全耗费在字句上头。」
「你叫我欢喜，」那女人喃喃道，「你叫我欢喜；你可肯到我这儿来，让我讲一个故事给你听，与我今夜你给我们的这首诗相配？」
她那语调里那种颤动的急切，简直无从描摹。宝拉为之震动。「倘若你肯告诉我你是谁，」宝拉说，「我必当设法前来。凡你愿意对我讲的，我都乐于一听。」
「我原以为人人都晓得我是谁。」那女人答道；她把宝拉拉回前厅，把脸朝她转了过来。「随便哪一位都能告诉你，玛乔丽·哈姆林（Margery Hamlin）住在哪儿。」她说，「可别叫我失望，也别叫我等得太久。」说罢，她颔一颔首，露出一抹深沉而古怪的笑——那一笑，竟叫她那张苍老的脸近乎年轻了起来——便步入人群，从宝拉的视野中消失了。

===Original===
It was the woman whose nightly visits to the deserted home of the Japhas had once been the talk and was still the unsolved mystery of the town.

===Chinese===
这正是那个女人——她夜夜探访雅法家那座空宅的举动，曾经是满城物议的话题，至今仍是这镇上一桩悬而未决的疑团。

## V The Rubicon / 五 卢比孔河

===Original===
> "I'll stake my life upon her faith."

Once convinced of the identity of my sweet young friend with the Miss Preston at whose feet a two year hence, the wealth and aristocracy of New York would be kneeling, I drew back from further effort as having received a damper to my presumptuous hopes that would soon effectually stifle them. Everything I heard about the family—and it seemed as if suddenly each chance acquaintance that I met had something to say about Mr. Preston either as a banker or a man, only served to confirm me in this view. "He is a money worshipper," said one. "The bluest of blue Presbyterians," declared another. "The enemy of presumption and anything that looks like an overweening confidence in one's own worth or capabilities," remarked a third. "A man who would beggar himself to save the honor of a corporation with which he was concerned," observed a fourth "but who would not invite to his table the most influential man connected with it if that man was unable to trace his family back to the old Dutch settlers to which Mr. Preston's own ancestors belonged."

This latter statement I have no doubt was exaggerated for I myself have seen him at dinners where half the gentlemen who lifted the wine glass were self-made in every sense of the term. But it showed the bent of his mind and it was a bent that left me entirely out of the sweep of his acquaintanceship much less that of his exquisite daughter, the pride of his soul if not the jewel of his heart.

===Chinese===
> 「我愿以性命担保她的信义。」

一旦确认了我那位可爱的小友就是那位普雷斯顿小姐——两年之后，纽约的财富与名流都将跪倒在她脚下——我便收手不再作进一步的努力，因为我那僭妄的奢望已受了一记重压，不久便会被彻底扼杀。我所听到的关于这一家的一切——仿佛突然之间，我遇见的每一个泛泛之交都有话说，不是讲普雷斯顿先生作为银行家的一面，便是讲他作为普通人的一面——都只是更加坚定了我这一看法。「他是个拜金的人。」一个说。「最最刻板的长老会教徒。」另一个断言。「凡是僭妄之举、凡是看着像是过分自信于自身价值或才干的东西，他一概是敌人。」第三个评论道。「一个为了保全他所关联的某家公司的名誉，不惜倾家荡产的人，」第四个说道，「但他绝不会请与他共事的最有影响的人物上自己的餐桌，倘若那人不能把自己的家世追溯到那些荷兰早期移民——普雷斯顿先生自己的祖先便在其中——的话。」

这后一种说法，我毫不怀疑，是言过其实的，因为我自己就曾见过他出席的宴会，在那里举杯的绅士有一半都是地地道道白手起家的人。但这至少透露了他心性的取向，而这一取向使我完全落在他交往的范围之外，更不必说落在他那精致的女儿——纵然不是他心中的珍宝，也是他灵魂的骄傲——的交往范围之外了。

===Original===
But when will a man who has seen or who flatters himself that he has seen in the eyes of the woman he admires, the least spark of that fire which is consuming his own soul, pause at an obstacle which after all has its basis simply in circumstances of position or will. By the time the two weeks of her expected absence had expired, I had settled it in my own mind that I would see her again and if I found the passing caprice of a child was likely to blossom into the steady regard of a woman, risk all in the attempt to win by honorable endeavor and persistence this bud of loveliness for my future wife.

How I finally succeeded by means of my friend Farrar in being one evening invited to the same house as Miss Preston it is not necessary to state. You will believe me it was done with the utmost regard for her feelings and in a way that deceived Farrar himself, who if he is the most prying is certainly the most volatile of men. In a crowded parlor, then, in the midst of the flash of diamonds and the flutter of fans Miss Preston and I again met. When I first saw her she was engaged in conversation with some young companion, and I had the pleasure of watching for a few minutes, unobserved, the play of her ingenuous countenance, as she talked with her friend, or sat silently watching the brilliant array before her. I found her like and yet unlike the vision of my dreams. More blithesome in her appearance, as was not strange considering her party attire and the lustre of the chandelier under which she sat, there was still that indescribable something in her expression which more than the flash of her eye or the curve of her lip, though both were lovely to me, made her face the one woman's face in the world for me; a charm which circumstances might alter, or suffering impair, but of which nothing save death could ever completely divest her and not death either, for it was the seal of her individuality, and that she would take with her into the skies.

===Chinese===
然而，一个男子若是看见、或自以为看见了他所倾慕的女子眼中那一星足以吞噬自己灵魂的火焰，又怎会因一道障碍而却步——何况这道障碍归根结底不过是处境或意愿上的事。等到她预计外出的两个星期期满，我已在心里打定主意：我要再见她一面；若我发现一个孩子一时的痴念有望绽放为一个成年女子笃定的情意，我便要孤注一掷，以光明正大的努力与坚持，去赢取这朵含苞的可爱做我未来的妻子。

至于我最后如何借助我的朋友法拉尔（Farrar）之力，在一个夜晚被邀进了普雷斯顿小姐也在的同一户人家，就不必细说了。你该相信我，这事做得极为顾及她的感受，而且做得连法拉尔本人也瞒过了——他纵然是最爱刺探隐私的人，却也定然是最心性浮躁的人。于是在一间宾客拥挤的客厅里，在钻石的闪烁与折扇的翻飞之中，普雷斯顿小姐与我再度相遇。我初见她时，她正与一位年轻的女伴交谈，我便有幸在没人留意时，观察了几分钟她那天真面容的神情变化——看她与朋友说话，或静静地坐着，望着眼前那一片珠光宝气的人群。我觉得她既像、又不像我梦中所见的那个身影。她的容止比我梦中更为明朗快活——考虑到她一身赴宴的盛装、她头顶那盏枝形吊灯的辉光，这并不奇怪——然而她神情之中仍有一种难以言喻的东西，胜过她眼波的流转或唇线的曲度——尽管这两样在我看来都可爱——使她的脸成为世上于我而言唯一的女子之面；这是一种境遇或许能改变、苦难或许能损伤的魅力，但除了死亡，没有任何东西能将它从她身上彻底剥离——甚至死亡也不能，因为那是她独一无二之天性的印记，她将把它一并带入天国。

===Original===
"If I might but advance and sit down by her side without a word of explanation or the interference of conventionalities how happy I should be," thought I. But I knew that would not do, so I contented myself with my secret watch over her movements, longing for and yet dreading the advance of my hostess, with its inevitable introduction. Suddenly the piano was touched in a distant room and not till I saw the quick change in her face, a change hard to explain, did I recognize the selection as one I was in the habit of playing. *She* had not forgotten at least, and thrilled by the thought and the remembrance of that surge of color which had swept like a flood over her cheek, I turned away, feeling as if I were looking on what it was for no man's eyes to see, least of all mine.

My hostess' voice arrested me and next moment I was bowing to the ground before Miss Preston.

===Chinese===
「要是我能径直走上前去，无须一句解释、无须任何客套的阻隔，在她身旁坐下，那该多么幸福。」我心想。但我知道这不行，于是我便满足于悄悄留意她的一举一动，既盼着、又惧怕女主人的走近以及随之而来不可避免的引见。忽然，远处一间屋子里有人弹起了钢琴；直到我看见她脸上那难以解释的迅速变化，我才认出那支曲子正是我惯常弹奏的一首。至少*她*没有忘记；这一念头，加上回想起方才像潮水般涌过她脸颊的那片红晕，令我心潮激荡，我转过身去，觉得自己仿佛窥见了一样本不该为任何男子所见的东西——尤其不该为我所见。

女主人的声音唤住了我，紧接着我便在普雷斯顿小姐面前深鞠到地。

===Original===
I am not a boy; nor have I been without my experiences: life with its vicissitudes has taught me many a lesson, subjected me to many a trial, yet in all my career have I never known a harder moment than when I raised my eyes to meet hers after that lowly obeisance. That she would be indignant I knew, that she might even misinterpret my motives and probably withdraw without giving me an opportunity to speak, I felt to be only too probable, but that she would betray an agitation so painful I had not anticipated, and for an instant I felt that I had hazarded my life's happiness on a cast that was going against me. But the necessity of saving her from remark speedily restored me to myself, and following the line of conduct I had previously laid out, I addressed her with the reserve of a stranger, and neither by word, look or manner conveyed to her a suggestion that we had ever met or spoken to each other before. She seemed to appreciate my consideration and though she was as yet too much unused to the ways of the world to completely hide her perturbation, she gradually regained a semblance of self-possession, and ere long was enabled to return short answers to my remarks, though her eyes remained studiously turned aside and never so much as ventured to raise themselves to the passing throng much less to my face, half turned away also.

Presently however a change passed over her. Pressing her two little hands together, she drew back a step or two, speaking my name with a certain tone of command. Struck with apprehension, I knew not why, I followed her. Instantly like one repeating a lesson she spoke.

===Chinese===
我不是个孩子了；我也并非没有阅历：生活及其沧桑教了我许多功课，让我受了种种试炼，然而在我全部的经历中，我从不知有哪个时刻比我行过那一躬、抬眼去迎她的目光时更艰难。我知道她会恼怒，我也觉得她很有可能曲解我的用意，甚至可能不等我有开口的机会便抽身离去；但她竟会流露出那样痛苦的激动，却是我所未曾预料的，有那么一瞬，我觉得自己已把一生的幸福押上了一注正在反水的骰子。但必须救她免于旁人议论的必要，迅速使我恢复了镇定；我循着先前定下的方针，以一个陌生人的矜持与她说话，无论言语、目光或举止都不曾向她暗示我们曾经相见或交谈过。她似乎体谅我的这份周全，尽管她还太不谙世事、无法完全掩饰自己的慌乱，却渐渐找回了自持的表象，不久便能对我的话作简短的回答，虽然她的眼睛始终刻意地偏向一旁，绝不敢抬起来去看一来一往的人群，更不敢看向我那也半转开去的脸。

然而不久，她身上掠过一层变化。她把两只小手紧紧攥在一起，退后一两步，用一种近乎命令的口气唤我的名字。我莫名地心生忧虑，不知为何，便跟了上去。她立刻像背书一般说起话来。

===Original===
"It is very good in you to talk to me as though we were the strangers that people believe us. I appreciate it and thank you very much. But it is not being just true; that is I feel as if I were not being just true, and as we can never be friends, would it not be better for us not to meet in this way any more?"

"And why," I gently asked, with a sense of struggling for my life, "can we never be friends?"

Her answer was a deep blush; not that timid conscious appeal of the blood that is beating too warmly for reply, but the quick flush of indignant generosity forced to do despite to its own instincts.

"That is a question I would rather not answer," she murmured at length. "Only it is so; or I should not speak in this way."

===Chinese===
「您肯这样和我说话，仿佛我们是众人所以为的那样的陌生人，您真好。我很感激，十分谢谢您。但这样做并不算完全真诚；我是说我好像觉得并不算真诚，既然我们永远不可能做朋友，那我们今后不再这样相见，岂不是更好吗？」

「那又是为什么，」我轻声问，怀着一种为自己的性命挣扎之感，「我们永远不可能做朋友呢？」

她的回答是一阵深深的涨红；不是那种血气太旺、情怯不敢作答的羞怯之色，而是一种出于愤慨的慷慨之气，被逼迫着违背自己本能时涌起的急潮。

「这个问题我宁愿不作回答，」她终于低声说。「只是事情就是这样；不然我也不会这样说话。」

===Original===
"But," I ventured, resolved to know on just what foundations my happiness was tottering, "you will at least tell me if this harsh decree is owing to any offence I myself may have inadvertently given. The honor of your acquaintance," I went on, determined she should know just what a hope she was slaying, "is much too earnestly desired, for me to wilfully hazard its loss by saying or doing aught that could be in any way displeasing to you."

"You have done nothing but what was generous," said she with increasing womanliness of manner, "unless it was taking advantage of my being here, to learn my name and gain an introduction to me after I had desired you to forget my very existence."

I recoiled at that, the chord of my self-respect was touched. "It was not here I learned your name, Miss Preston. It has been known to me for two weeks. At the risk of losing by your displeasure what is already hazarded by your prudence, I am bound to acknowledge that from the hour I left your father's house that night, I have spared no effort compatible with my deep respect for your feelings, to ascertain who the young lady was that had done me such an honor, and won from me such a deep regard. I had not intended to tell you this," I added, "but your truth has awakened mine, and whatever the result may be, you must see me as I am."

===Chinese===
「但是，」我斗胆说道，决意要弄清我的幸福究竟在怎样的根基上摇摇欲坠，「您至少该告诉我，这道严苛的判决，是不是因为我自己不慎冒犯了您。与您结识的这份荣幸，」我接着说，决意让她知道自己正在扼杀的是怎样一种希望，「是我所极其珍重地渴求着的，我绝不会故意地以任何言语或行为冒犯您，从而拿它的失去来冒险。」

「您所做的一切，除了一件以外，都是宽厚的，」她带着越发深沉的成年女子气度说，「那唯一的一件，便是趁着我今晚在场之机，打听出我的姓名，求人把我介绍给您——而那是在我请求您忘记我这个人存在之后。」

听到这话我退了一步，自尊这根弦被触动了。「我并不是在这里才得知您的姓名的，普雷斯顿小姐。我已经知道它两个星期了。冒着因您的不快而失去——您的小心谨慎已令其岌岌可危——的东西的风险，我必须承认：从那天夜里我离开您父亲家的那一刻起，我便在深重尊重您感受的前提下，不遗余力地查明这位赏我如此殊荣、赢得我如此深重情意的小姐究竟是谁。我本不打算告诉您这些，」我补充道，「但您的真诚唤醒了我的真诚，无论结果如何，您都必须照我本来的样子看待我。」

===Original===
"You are very kind," she replied governing with growing skill the trembling of her voice. "The acquaintance of a girl of sixteen is not worth so much trouble on the part of a man like yourself." And blushing with the vague apprehension of her sex in the presence of a devotion she rather feels than understands, she waved her trembling little hand and paused irresolute, seemingly anxious to terminate the interview but as yet too inexperienced to know how to manage a dismissal requiring so much tact and judgment.

I saw, comprehended her position and hesitated. She was so young, uncle, her prospects in life were so bright; if I left her then, in a couple of weeks she would forget me. What was I that I should throw the shadow of manhood's deepest emotion across the paradise of her young untrammelled being. But the old Adam of selfishness has his say in my soul as well as in that of my fellow-men, and forgetting myself enough to glance at her half averted face, I could not remember myself sufficiently afterwards to forego without a struggle, all hope of some day beholding that soft cheek turn in confidence at my approach.

"Miss Preston," said I, "the promise of the bud atones for its folded leaves." Then with a fervor I did not seek to disguise, "You say we cannot be friends; would your decision be the same if this were our first meeting?"

Again that flush of outraged feeling. "I don't know—yes I think—I fear it would."

===Chinese===
「您太客气了，」她答道，越发娴熟地压住了声音的颤抖。「一个十六岁姑娘的相识，不值得像您这样的人费这样大的周折。」她涨红了脸——那是她的性别在一股她隐约感到、却还未能理解的倾慕之前那种朦胧的惶恐——她挥了挥那只发颤的小手，踌躇着停下，似乎急于结束这场谈话，却又太没经验，不知该如何得体而周全地把人打发走。

我看出了，也体谅她的处境，犹豫了。她那样年轻，叔叔，她的前程那样光明；倘若我那时便离去，不出两个星期她便会忘掉我。我算什么人，竟该把成年男子最深重的情感的阴影，投到她那少女无拘束的天堂之上？但那自私的「旧人」在我的灵魂里，正如在他人灵魂里一样，也有它的一席之地；我足以忘怀自己而去瞥她那半转开的脸，之后却再不能足够地记起自己，从而毫无挣扎地放弃某一日看见那柔嫩面颊在我走近时信赖地转过来的一切希望。

「普雷斯顿小姐，」我说，「花蕾的允诺，足以补偿它合拢的花瓣。」随即以一种我不加掩饰的热忱：「您说我们不能做朋友；倘若这是我们头一次相见，您的决定还会一样吗？」

又是一阵受委屈之情的潮红。「我不知道——是的我以为——我恐怕会一样。」

===Original===
I strove to help her. "There is too great a difference between Bertram Mandeville the pianist, and the daughter of Thaddeus Preston."

She turned and looked me gently in the eye, she did not need to speak. Regret, shame, longing flashed in her steady glance.

"Do not answer," said I, "I understand; I am glad it is circumstances that stand in the way, and not any misconception on your part as to my motives and deep consideration for yourself. Circumstances can be changed." And satisfied with having thus dropped into the fruitful soil of that tender breast, the seed of a future hope, I bowed with all the deference at my command and softly withdrew.

But not to rest. With all the earnestness with which a man sets himself to decide upon the momentous question of life or death, I gave myself up to a night of reflection, and seated in my solitary bachelor apartment, debated with myself as to the resolution at which I had dimly hinted in my parting words to Miss Preston.

===Chinese===
我试图帮她一把。「钢琴家贝特拉姆·曼德维尔，与撒迪厄斯·普雷斯顿（Thaddeus Preston）的女儿之间，差别实在太大了。」

她转过脸来，温柔地看着我的眼睛，她不必开口。遗憾、羞愧、渴慕，一一在她沉静的目光中闪过。

「不必回答，」我说，「我明白了；我很高兴挡在路上的，是境遇，而不是您对我的用意以及对您自己的深切体谅有什么误解。境遇是可以改变的。」我对自己就这样把一颗未来希望的种子，投进了那温柔胸怀的沃土里感到满意，便尽我所能地谦恭鞠了一躬，悄然退去。

但退去并非为了歇息。我以一种男子决断生死大计般的全部郑重，把自己交给了一个不眠之夜的思量；我独自坐在单身汉的寓所里，反复权衡着我临别时对普雷斯顿小姐含糊暗示过的那个决心。

===Original===
That I am a musician by nature, my success with the public seems to indicate. That by following out the line upon which I had entered I would attain a certain eminence in my art, I do not doubt. But uncle, there are two kinds of artists in this world; those that work because the spirit is in them and they cannot be silent if they would, and those that speak from a conscientious desire to make apparent to others the beauty that has awakened their own admiration. The first could not give up his art for any cause, without the sacrifice of his soul's life; the latter—well the latter could and still be a man with his whole inner being intact. Or to speak plainer, the first has no choice, while the latter has, if he has a will to exert it. Now you will say, and the world at large, that I belong to the former class. I have risen in ten years from a choir boy in Trinity Church to a position in the world of music that insures me a full audience wherever and whenever I have a mind to exert my skill as a pianist. Not a man of my years has a more promising outlook in my profession, if you will pardon the seeming egotism of the remark, and yet by the ease with which I felt I could give it up at the first touch of a master passion, I know that I am not a prophet in my art but merely an interpreter, one who can speak well but who has never felt the descent of the burning tongue and hence not a sinner against my own soul if I turn aside from the way I am walking. The question was, then, should I make a choice?

===Chinese===
我天生是个音乐家——我在公众中的成功似乎正说明了这一点。沿着我所踏入的这条路走下去，我会在我的艺术中达到相当的高度，这一点我并不怀疑。但是叔叔，世上的艺术家有两类：一类是因为灵感在体内、想沉默也无法沉默才创作的；另一类则是出于一种诚挚的愿望——要把唤醒自己赞叹之情的美好，也向他人显现出来——才开口的。前者无论为了什么缘故都不能放弃他的艺术，否则便要牺牲他灵魂的生命；后者——嗯，后者却可以放弃，而且放弃之后仍不失为一个内心完整的人。说得更明白些：前者无从选择，而后者是有选择的——只要他肯运用自己的意志。如今你，以及世上的大多数人，都会说我属于前一类。十年来我已从三一教堂的一名唱诗班男童，升到了音乐界中这样一个位置——无论何时何地，只要我愿意以钢琴家的身份施展技艺，都保准有满座的听众。在我这个年纪，同行中没有谁的专业前景比我更可观了——请原谅这句话看似自大——然而，从我在一股主宰性激情初触之下便感到自己竟能轻而易举地放弃它的那份轻松之中，我知道我在艺术中并非先知，而只是一个诠释者：一个能说得好、却从未感到那燃烧的舌头降临的人；因此，倘若我从正走着的路上转开，我也并未背叛自己的灵魂。问题于是成了：我该不该作一个抉择？

===Original===
Love, as you say, seems at first blush too insecure a joy, if not often too trivial a one, to unsettle a man in his career and change the bent of his whole after life; especially a love born of surprise and fed by the romance of distance and mystery. Had I met her in ordinary intercourse, surrounded by her friends and without the charm cast over her by unwonted circumstances, and then had felt as I did now that of all women I had seen, she alone would ever move the deep springs of my being, it would be different. But with this atmosphere of romance surrounding and hallowing her girl's form till it seemed almost as ethereal and unearthly as that of an angel's, was I safe in risking fame or fortune in an attempt to acquire what in the possession might prove as bare and commonplace as a sweep of mountain heather stripped of its sunshine. Curbing every erratic beat of my heart, I summoned up her image as it bloomed in my fancy, and surveying it with cruel eyes, asked what was real and what the fruit of my own imagination. The gentle eye, the trembling lip, the girlish form eloquent with the promise of coming womanhood—were these so rare, that beside them no other woman should seem to glance or smile or move? And her words! what had she said, that any simple-minded, modest yet loving girl might not have uttered under the circumstances. Surely my belief in her being the one, the best and the dearest was a delusion, and to no delusion was I willing to sacrifice my art.

===Chinese===
爱，正如你所说，乍看之下是一种太不牢靠的快乐——若不是说常常太轻浮的一种——不足以搅乱一个男子的前程、改变他整个余生的心志所向；尤其是一种生于意外、靠距离与神秘的浪漫气氛滋养起来的爱。倘若我是在寻常的交往中遇见她，她置身于自己的朋友之间、没有那一反常态的境遇为她披上的魅力，然后我才感到如同现在这般——在我所见的一切女子中，唯有她能触动我生命深处的那几根弦——那就不同了。可是，有这一重浪漫的氛围环绕着、圣化着她那少女的身形，直到它看上去几乎如天使一般空灵出尘——我把名声与 fortune 一并押上，去争取一件也许一旦拥有便如一片被剥去了阳光的山坡石楠花一般寡淡平庸的东西，这样冒险稳妥吗？我压下心脏每一阵任性的跳动，唤出她在我幻想中绽放的模样，用冷酷的目光打量它，问自己什么是真实的、什么又是我自己想象的产物。那温柔的眼睛、那颤动的嘴唇、那少女的身姿——其中饱含着行将到来的成年女子之态的允诺——这些果真稀罕到，除她之外再没有别的女子看来能一顾、一笑、一动了吗？还有她说的话！她说过哪一句，是任何心地单纯、矜持却深情的姑娘在那样的情境下不会说出口的呢？我认定她是那唯一的一个、最好也最珍贵的那个，这无疑是一种妄想，而任何妄想我都不愿为之牺牲我的艺术。

===Original===
But straight upon that conclusion came sweeping down a flood of counter-reasons. If not the wonder she seemed, she was at least a wonder to me. If I had seen her under romantic circumstances, and unconsciously been influenced by them, the influence had remained and nothing would ever rob her form of the halo thus acquired. Whether I ever won her to my fireside or not, she must always remain the fairy figure of my dreams, and being so, the gentle eye and tender lip acquired a value that made them what they seemed, the exponent of love and happiness. And lastly if love well or illy founded was an uncertain joy, and the passion for a woman a poor substitute for the natural incentive of talent or ambition, *this* love had within it the beginning of something deeper than joy, and in the passion thus cheaply characterized, dwelt a force and living fire that notwithstanding all I have hitherto achieved, has ever been lacking from my dreams of endeavor.

As you will see, the most natural question of all did not disturb me in these cogitations: And that was, whether in making the sacrifice I proposed, I should meet with the reward I had promised myself. The fancies of a young girl of sixteen are not usually of a stable enough character to warrant a man in building upon them his whole future happiness, especially a young girl situated like Miss Preston in the midst of friends who would soon be admirers, and adulators who would soon be her humble slaves. But the doubt which a serious contemplation of this risk must have presented, was of so unnerving a character, I dared not admit it. *If* I made the sacrifice, I must meet with my reward. I would listen to no other conclusion.

===Chinese===
然而紧随这一结论而来的，是一股反方向的思潮席卷而下。纵然她不是她看来的那个奇迹，至少对我而言，她是一个奇迹。纵然我是在浪漫的情境中遇见了她、在不知不觉中受了那些情境的影响，这影响却已留存下来，再没有什么能剥夺她的身形由此获得的那道光晕。无论我日后能否把她赢到我的炉边，她都必将永远是我梦中那个仙子般的身影；既然如此，那温柔的眼睛和柔嫩的嘴唇便获得了一种价值，使它们当真成了它们看来的那种样子——爱与幸福的化身。最后，纵然根基或深或浅的爱都是一种不牢靠的快乐，对一个女子的激情也只是才华或抱负之天然驱动力的拙劣替代，可*这一份*爱之中却孕育着某种比快乐更深的东西的开端；而在被如此轻描淡写地称作的这份激情里，蕴藏着一种力量与活火——它是我迄今为止的一切成就所不曾有的，也是我种种奋进之梦中所一直欠缺的。

正如你会看到的，在这些思量中，那个最自然不过的问题竟没有搅扰我：那便是，在我作出我所打算的牺牲之后，我是否真能得到我向自己允诺的酬报。一个十六岁少女的痴念，通常都不够稳固，不足以使一个男子把整个未来的幸福建立在上面；尤其是一个处境如普雷斯顿小姐那样的少女——她置身于不久便将成为爱慕者的朋友之中，以及不久便将成为她卑微奴仆的谄媚者之中。但凡认真思量这一风险所必然生出的疑虑，其性质都足以令人丧胆，我不敢让它进门。*如果*我作出了牺牲，我就必定会得到我的酬报。任何别样的结论我都不愿听。

===Original===
Besides, something in the young girl herself, I cannot tell what, assured me then as it assures me now, that whatever virtues or graces she might lack, that of fidelity to a noble idea was not among them; that once convinced of the purity and value of the flame that had been lit in her innocent breast, nothing short of the unworthiness of the object that had awakened it, would ever serve to eliminate or extinguish it. That I was not worthy but would make it the business of my life to become so, was certain; that she would mark my endeavors and bestow upon me the sympathy they deserved, I was equally sure. No one would ever make such a sacrifice to her love as I was willing to do, and consequently in no one would I find a rival.

The morning light surprised me in the midst of the struggle, nor did I decide the question that day. Mr. Preston might not be as determined in his prejudices against musicians as my friends or even his daughter had imagined. I resolved to see him. Taking advantage of his connection with the ——— Club, I procured an introducer in the shape of a highly respected person of his own class, and went one evening to the Club-rooms with the full intention of making his acquaintance if possible. He was already there and in conversation with some business associates. Procuring a seat as near him as possible, I anxiously surveyed his countenance. It was not a reassuring one, and studied in this way, had the effect of dampening any hopes I may have cherished in the outset. He soften to the sounds of sweet strains or the voice of youthful passion! As soon the granite rock to the surge of the useless billow. His very necktie spoke volumes. It was an old fashioned stock, full of the traditions of other days, while his coat, shabbier than any I would presume to wear, betrayed in every well-worn seam the pride of the aristocrat and millionaire who in his native city and before the eyes of his fellow magnates does not need to carry the evidences of his respectability upon his back.

===Chinese===
况且，这少女身上的某种东西——我说不清是什么——当时就像现在一样使我相信：无论她可能欠缺怎样的美德或风采，对一项崇高理想的忠贞都不在其中；一旦她确信那在她天真胸怀中被点燃的火焰之纯洁与可贵，那么，除了唤起它的那个对象的不堪之外，再没有别的什么能将它消除或扑灭。我是不堪配的，但我会把成为堪配之人当作毕生的事业，这是确定的；而她会留意我的努力、给予它们应得的体谅，我同样确信。再没有谁会像我情愿的那样，为她的爱作出这样的牺牲，因此再没有谁会成为我的对手。

晨光在这场挣扎之中照见了我，那一天我并未把问题决定下来。普雷斯顿先生对音乐家的成见，也许并不像我的朋友们、乃至他的女儿所以为的那样根深蒂固。我决意去见一见他。借着他在——俱乐部的那层关系，我请到了一位同阶级中深受敬重的人物做我的引介人，于某日傍晚走进俱乐部会所，存着若有可能便与他结识的充分打算。他已经在那里了，正与几位生意上的同人交谈。我在离他尽可能近的地方觅了一个座位，焦灼地打量他的面容。那并不是一副令人宽慰的面容，这样端详下来，倒把我起初也许怀有的几分希望浇熄了。他会为甜美乐音或少年激情之声而心软！那简直同花岗岩石对无谓浪潮的拍打动容一样不可能。单是他那条领巾便胜过千言万语。那是一条老式的高领巾，饱含着旧日时光的传统；而他的外套，比我自问敢于穿的任何一件都更寒酸，却在每一道磨旧的衣缝里，暴露出一个贵族兼百万富翁的骄傲——这样一个人在自己的本城、在与其并肩的同侪巨子们眼前，是不必把体面的证据穿在背上的。

===Original===
"It would be worse than folly for me to approach him on such a subject," I mentally ejaculated. "If he did not stare the musician out of countenance he would the newly risen man." And I came very near giving up the whole thing.

But the genius that watches over the affairs of true love was with me notwithstanding the unpropitious state of my surroundings. In a few minutes I received my expected introduction to Mr. Preston, and I found that underneath the repelling austerity of his expression, was a kindly spark for youth, and a decided sympathy for all instances of manly endeavor if only it was in a direction he approved; further that my own personality was agreeable to him and that he was disposed to regard me with favor until by some chance and very natural allusion to my profession by the friend standing between us, he learned that I was a musician, when a decided change came over his countenance and he exclaimed in that blunt, decisive way of his that admits of no reply:

"A jingler on the piano, eh? Pretty poor use for a man to put his brains to, I say, or even his fingers. Sorry to hear we cannot be friends." And without waiting for a reply, took my introducer by the arm and drew him a step or so to one side. "Why didn't you say at once he was Mandeville the musician," I overheard him ask in somewhat querulous tones. "Don't you know I consider the whole race of them an abomination. I would have more respect for my bank clerk than I would for the greatest man of them all, were it Rubenstein himself." Then in a lower tone but distinctly and almost as if he meant me to hear, "My daughter has a leaning towards this same fol-de-rol and has lately requested my permission to make the acquaintance of some musical characters, but I soon convinced her that manhood under the disguise of a harlequin's jacket could have no interest for her; that when a human being, man or woman has sunk to be a mere rattler of sweet sounds, he has reached a stage of infantile development that has little in common with the nervous energy and business force of her Dutch ancestry. And my daughter stoops to make no acquaintances she cannot bid sit at her father's table."

===Chinese===
「我去就这种事接近他，简直比徒劳还不如，」我在心里脱口而出。「他纵然不因音乐家这一点而把我盯得无地自容，也会因我是个新起家的人而这么做。」我差一点就把整件事放弃了。

然而，纵然我周遭的处境如此不利，那守护真爱之事的 Genius 仍与我同在。不多时我便如期得到了对普雷斯顿先生的引见，我发现，在他那拒人于千里之外的严峻神情之下，藏着一星对青年的善意之火，以及对一切男子气概之奋进的明确同情——只要那奋进的方向是他赞成的；此外，我这个人本身也合他的意，他也存着几分青眼看待我，直到站在我们之间的那位朋友，偶然而又十分自然地提及我的职业，他方才得知我是个音乐家——这时他脸上便掠过一层明显的变化，并以他那种不许人回嘴的生硬、决断的口吻嚷道：

「是个在钢琴上叮叮咚咚的，嗯？我说，把脑筋花在这上头，太没出息了，就连把指头花在这上头也是。听说我们做不成朋友了，真遗憾。」不等回答，他便挽起我那位引介人的胳膊，把他拉到一旁一两步。「你怎么不早说他是音乐家曼德维尔呢，」我听见他用几分埋怨的口气问。「你难道不知道我觉得这帮人全都是可憎之物吗？哪怕其中最了不起的人，哪怕他是鲁宾斯坦（Rubenstein）本人，我对自家银行里的小职员都比对他更尊重些。」随即，他换了一种更低、却分明清晰、几乎像是存心要我听见的声调：「我女儿偏偏也偏向这种花哨玩意儿，近来还请求我准许她结识几个搞音乐的人物，可我不久便使她明白：裹在小丑外套之下的男子气概对她不可能有什么吸引力；一个人，无论男女，一旦沦落到不过是个拨弄悦耳声响的，便已退化到了一种幼童阶段，与她那荷兰祖先的刚健精力与办事魄力没什么共通之处了。我女儿也从不肯屈尊去结交任何她不能请到她父亲餐桌上就座的人。」

===Original===
"Your daughter is a child yet, I thought," was ventured by his companion.

"Miss Preston is sixteen, just the age at which my mother gave her hand to my respected father sixty-seven years ago." And with this drop of burning lead let fall into my already agitated bosom they passed on.

He would have more respect for his bank clerk! Would his bank clerk or what was better, a young man with means at his command, working in a business capacity more in consonance with the tastes he had evinced, have a chance of winning his daughter? I began to think he might. "The way grows clearer!" I exclaimed.

But it was not till after another interview with him ten minutes later in the lobby that I finally made up my mind. He was standing quite alone in an obscure corner, fumbling in an awkward way with his muffler that had caught on the button of his coat. Seeing it, I hastened forward to his assistance and was rewarded by a kind enough nod to embolden me to say,

"I have been introduced to you as a musician; would my acquaintance be more acceptable to you if I told you that the pursuit of art bids fair in my case to yield to the exigencies of business? That I purpose leaving the concert-room for the banker's office and that henceforth my only ambition promises to be that of Wall Street?"

"It most certainly would," exclaimed he, holding out his hand with an unmistakable gesture of satisfaction. "You have too good a countenance to waste before a piano-top strumming to the smirks of women and the plaudits of weak-headed men. Let us see you at the desk, my lad. We are in want of trustworthy young men to take the place of us older ones." Then politely, "Do you expect to make the change soon?"

"I do," said I.

And the Rubicon was passed.

===Chinese===
「我原以为令嫒还是个孩子呢。」他的同伴大着胆子说了一句。

「普雷斯顿小姐十六岁了，恰好是六十七年前我母亲把她的一只手交给我的令尊时的年纪。」随着这一滴滚烫的铅落进我本已激荡的胸怀，他们走过去了。

他对自家银行里的小职员还更尊重些！那么他那位银行小职员，或者更理想些，一个手头宽裕、在更合他所表露之趣味的实业中任职的青年，可有赢得他女儿的机会？我开始觉得也许有。「路子越来越清楚了！」我叫出声来。

然而直到十分钟之后在门厅里与他又有一次照面，我才彻底打定了主意。他正独自站在一个不显眼的角落里，别扭地摆弄着缠在大衣纽扣上的围巾。我看见便赶上前去帮他解开，得到了一个足够和蔼的颔首作为回报，使我有胆量说道：

「我被引见给您时是个音乐家；倘若我告诉您，在我这里，对艺术的追求眼看要让位于实务的需要；我打算离开音乐厅、走进银行家的办公室，而且今后我唯一的抱负有望只是华尔街的那一套——那么，您是不是更愿意接纳我这份相识呢？」

「那自然是再好也没有了。」他嚷道，伸出手来，带着一种一望而知的满意。「你生了一副太好的面相，不该把它浪费在钢琴前面，对着女人们的媚笑和没头脑男人们的喝彩叮叮咚咚。让我们在办公桌前看到你吧，我的小伙子。我们正需要靠得住的青年来接替我们这些年长的人。」随即客气地补了一句：「你打算不久就改行吗？」

「我打算。」我说。

卢比孔河便这样渡过了。

## XVI The Sword of Damocles / 十六 达摩克利斯之剑

===Original===
> "And my imaginations are as foul

 As Vulcan's smithy."

> "Why, all the souls that were, were forfeit once;

 Found out the remedy."

Mrs. Sylvester reclining on the palest of blue couches, in the slanting sunlight of an April afternoon, is a study for a painter. Not that such inspiring loveliness breathed from her person, conspicuous as it was for its rich and indolent grace, but because in every attitude of her large and well formed limbs, in every raise of the thick white lids from eyes whose natural brightness was obscured by the mist of aimless fancies, she presented such an embodiment of luxurious ease, one might almost imagine they were gazing upon the favorite Sultana of some eastern court, or, to be for once poetical as the subject demands, a full blown Egyptian lotus floating in hushed enjoyment on the placid waters of its native stream. Indeed for all the blonde character of her beauty, there was certainly something oriental about the physique of this favored child of fortune. Had the tint of her skin been richened to a magnolia bloom instead of reminding you of that description accorded to the complexion of one of Napoleon's sisters, that it looked like white satin seen through pink glass, she would have passed in any Eastern market, for a rare specimen of Circassian beauty.

But Mr. Sylvester coming home fatigued and harassed, cared little for Circassian beauties or Oriental odalisques. It was a welcome that he desired, and such refreshment as a quick eye and ready hand can bestow when guided by a tender and loving heart; or so thought the watchful Paula as she glided from her room at the sound of his step in the hall, and met him coming weary and disheartened from the side of Ona's couch. The sight of her revived him at once.

===Chinese===
> 「我心中的想象，污浊如
> 武尔坎（Vulcan）的铁炉。」

> 「嗳，一切曾经存在的灵魂，都曾一度沦亡；
> 却寻得了救赎之道。」

四月午后斜斜的阳光里，西尔维斯特夫人（Mrs. Sylvester）斜倚在一张极淡的蓝色卧榻上，这一景本身就是画家一幅习作的好题材。倒不是她周身真有那样令人神往的美貌流溢——虽说那姿容确实以其浓艳而慵懒的风韵颇为惹眼——而是因为，她那一双丰腴而形态美好的肢体，无论作何姿态；那一双厚白的上眼睑，每当从双眸上抬起时——那眸子本来的明光，原已被一层漫无目的的幻想之雾遮蔽——所流露出的，都是那样一种雍容安逸的化身，叫人几乎以为自己正凝视着东方某座宫廷里最受宠的王后，或者，破例地像此情此景所要求的那样作一回诗人，把它比作一朵盛开的埃及莲花，在故土溪流那平缓的水面上悄然自得地随波浮荡。事实上，尽管她的美貌乃属金发碧眼一脉，这位命运的宠儿身形体格之中，确乎有几分东方气象。倘若她肌肤的色泽不是那副模样——叫人想起某位拿破仑（Napoleon）之妹肤色的那番形容，说它看上去活像隔着粉色玻璃看白缎子——而是再丰润些，润成木兰花开的那种颜色，那么她出现在东方任何一处市集上，都可作切爾克斯（Circassian）美人里罕见的一例而无人质疑。

可西尔维斯特先生（Mr. Sylvester）一身疲惫、满腹烦乱地回了家，哪里还有什么心情怀想切爾克斯美人或东方宫嫔。他所盼望的，不过是一声相迎，是一双明眼与一只快手——在一颗柔情蜜意之心的指引下——所能给予的那一份慰藉；或者，警醒的宝拉（Paula）是这么想的——她在房中听见他在门厅里的脚步声，便悄然溜了出来，迎上他从奥娜（Ona）的卧榻旁走过来，神情疲惫、意气消沉。一瞧见她，他便即刻精神一振。

===Original===
"Well, little one, what have you been doing today?"

Instantly a shade fell over her countenance. "I hardly know how to tell you. It has been a day of great experiences to me. I am literally shaken with them. I have been wanting to talk to Ona about what I have seen and heard, but thought I had best wait till you came home, for I could not repeat the story twice."

"What! you look pale. Nothing has happened to frighten you I hope," exclaimed he, leading her back to Ona's side, who stirred a little, and presently deigned to take an upright position.

===Chinese===
「嗳，小家伙，你今天都做什么来着？」

她脸上立时罩下一层阴影。「我几乎不知该怎样告诉你。这一日于我而言经历的种种实在太多了。我简直被它们震得七荤八素。我一直想同奥娜讲讲我所见所闻的事，可又觉得最好还是等你回家再说，因为那样一个故事，我没法说上两遍。」

「什么！你脸色不好。但愿没出什么吓着你的事。」他失声说道，牵着她的手引她回到奥娜身旁。奥娜稍稍动了动，过不多时，总算赏脸坐直了身。

===Original===
"I do not know if it is fear or horror," cried Paula, shuddering; "I have seen a fearful woman—But first I ought to tell you that I took a ride with Miss Stuyvesant in the Park this morning—"

"Yes, and persisted in going for that lady on horseback instead of sending the groom after her, and all starting from the front of our house," murmured Mrs. Sylvester with lazy chagrin.

Paula smiled, but otherwise took no notice of this standing topic of disagreement.

===Chinese===
「我不知那是恐惧还是骇然。」宝拉打着寒颤叫道，「我见到了一个可怖的女人——可我得先告诉你，今早我和斯泰弗森特小姐（Miss Stuyvesant）在公园里骑马来着——」

「不错，而且非得亲自骑着马去接那位小姐，不肯打发马夫去接，还偏要从我们家门口出发。」西尔维斯特夫人懒洋洋地咕哝着，语气里满是懊恼。

宝拉笑了笑，此外便不再理会这个素来争执的老话题。

===Original===
"It was a beautiful day," she proceeded, "and we enjoyed it very much, but we were so unfortunate as to run over a little boy, at that place where the equestrian road crosses the foot path; a lame child, Mr. Sylvester, who could not get out of our way; poor too, with a ragged jacket on which seemed to make it all the worse."

Ona gave a shrug with her white shoulders, that seemed to question this. "Did you injure him very much?" queried she, with a show of interest; not sufficient however to impair her curiosity as to the cut of one of her nails.

"I cannot say; his little arm was struck, and when I went to pick him up, he lay back in my lap and moaned till I thought my heart would break. But that was not the worst that happened. As we went hurrying up the walk to find the child's father, we were met by a woman wrapped in a black cloak whose long and greasy folds seemed like the symbol of her own untold depravity. Her glance as she encountered the child writhing in pain at my feet, made my heart stand still. It was more than malignant, it was actually fiendish. 'Is he hurt?' she asked, and it seemed as if she gloated over the question; she evidently longed to hear that he was, longed to be told that he would die; and when I inquired if she was his mother, she broke into a string of laughter, that seemed to darken the daylight. 'His mother! O yes, we look alike, don't we!' she exclaimed, pointing with a mocking gesture frightful to see, first at his eyes which were very blue and beautiful, and then at her own which were dark as evil thoughts could make them. I never saw anything so dreadful. Malignancy! and towards a little lame child! what could be more horrible!"

===Chinese===
「天气好极了，」她接着说，「我们玩得很是开心，可倒了大霉——在骑马道与步行道交错的那个地方，碾着了一个小男孩；是个瘸腿的孩子，西尔维斯特先生，他躲不开我们的路；还穷得很，身上一件破烂的小褂子，越发叫人看着难受。」

奥娜雪白的双肩微微一耸，似乎对此颇不以为然。「你伤着他了么？」她问道，做出一副关切的样子；可这点关切，尚不足以扰乱她对某一片指甲样式的琢磨之心。

「我说不好；他那只小胳膊被撞着了，我过去把他抱起来时，他仰躺在我腿上，一声声哼个不停，我听着心都快要碎了。可那还不是最糟的事。我们匆匆顺着步道跑去找孩子的父亲，迎面却遇上一个女人，裹着一件黑色斗篷，那斗篷又长又油腻的褶皱，活像她那不曾道尽的堕落本身的象征。她撞见那孩子在我脚边痛得打滚，向她投去的那一道目光，叫我的心都凝住了。那不止是恶毒，简直是恶魔一般。『他伤着了么？』她问，问时那神情，倒像是在幸灾乐祸；她分明巴不得听见他伤着了，巴不得有人告诉她他就要死了；等我开口问她是不是这孩子的母亲，她竟爆出一串大笑，那笑声仿佛把天光都染暗了。『他的母亲！嗳，是呀，我们长得像，不是么！』她失声叫道，一边用一种叫人不寒而栗的嘲弄手势，先是指那孩子那一双极蓝极美的眼睛，又指她自己的那一双——那双眼乌黑得正如邪念所能染就的那般乌黑。我从没见过这样可怖的事。那样的恶毒！还是对着一个瘸了腿的小孩！还有什么比这更骇人的！」

===Original===
Mr. Sylvester and his wife exchanged looks, then the former asked, "Did she follow you, Paula?"

"No; after telling me that I—But I cannot repeat what she said," exclaimed the young girl with a quick shudder. "Since I came home," she musingly continued, "I have looked and looked at my face in the glass, but I cannot believe that what she declared is true. There is no similarity between us, could never have been any: I will not have it that she ever saw in all the days of her life such a picture as that in her glass." And with a sudden gesture Paula started up and pointed to herself as she stood reflected in one of the tall mirrors with which Ona's boudoir abounded.

"And did she dare to make any comparison between you and her own degraded self?" exclaimed Mr. Sylvester, with a glance at the exquisite vision of pure girlhood thus doubly presented to his notice.

"Yes, what I am, she was once, or so she said. And it may be true.
